maintopic: VISIT TO TORONTO BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: VISIT TO TORONTO BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which I am sure that you and the house will willingly grant to me. You may have noticed that there were a few members absent from this chamber last Friday. The reason for their places being vacant was that the board of trade of the city of Toronto extended an invitation to the entire membership of the House of Commons to be their guests for three days this last week end.
Something over 130 members and their wives, amounting in all to a party of over 200 people, accepted that invitation. This visit to Toronto was one of the best good will trips which it has ever been our privilege to be associated with. It was handled from start to finish in a magnificent manner. On behalf of the members of the House of Commons who made this trip I want immediately to express our warmest appreciation to the board of trade for the arrangements made and the manner in which they were carried out. We spent three full days there, and every moment there was something planned for our enjoyment or something of interest for us to see.
While one would not wish to single out individuals, I do think that special reference should be made to Mr. Gerald Godsoe, president of the board of trade, and Mr. F. D. Tolchard its manager, who were mostly responsible for the arrangements. They were with us continuously, and did everything they could to make our visit both profitable and enjoyable. I think I should also mention the courtesy of the individual members of the board of trade in inviting members to their homes last evening. We from distant places are also indebted to the members of the House of Commons from Toronto who assisted in every way, thus adding to the pleasure of our trip, particularly in meeting their friends.
I think a special reference should be made to the Toronto transportation commission, which placed their buses at our service in the numerous trips we made throughout the
city, as well as the Toronto police commission, who saw to it that no one got lost or went astray.
We acknowledge as well the courtesies extended to us by His Honour the Lieutenant Governor, the premier and government of Ontario, the mayor and city council of Toronto, the Massey-Harris Company, Canada Packers Limited, A. V. Roe Canada Limited, the Toronto harbour commission, the management of Hart House, the staff of Sunnybrook hospital, and the Maple Leaf Gardens.
Of special interest to the ladies in the party, visits were arranged to the Toronto art gallery, the Sick Children's hospital, Sunnybrook hospital, and the Royal Ontario museum.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, you will appreciate knowing that the programs handed to us on our arrival were printed in both French and English.
This brief acknowledgment does not permit one to say all that should be said. There are, however, two items of sufficient general interest which might properly be mentioned-One is the Regent park housing development, and the other the Toronto rapid transit system. When some of us visited Toronto three years ago these developments were being talked about and planned. Today they-are both well under way. The Regent park: housing development is one of the first joint undertakings looking towards the removal of slum dwellings and replacing them by fully modern low rental housing units. The rapid transit underground development is the first of its kind to be attempted in the Dominion of Canada, and reflects great credit to the people of Toronto for their faith and foresight in looking to the future.
The city of Toronto, Mr. Speaker, "sold" Toronto to the membership of the House of Commons in a magnificent manner, and in so doing has given the people of other parts of Canada, from the Yukon and Mackenzie territories to our baby sister province of Newfoundland, an opportunity of seeing something of the problems of a large and growing industrial city, and how it attacks them. Toronto has of course long been recognized as the leading industrial and financial centre of Canada, with connections all over the country and in many places outside of Canada. It is recognized as well as

Parliamentarians' Visit to Toronto the educational and cultural centre, at least for the English-speaking portion of our population. It has kept itself well to the forefront through its two annual exhibitions, its international trade fair, and the numerous conventions which have selected Toronto as their meeting place. It is also recognized as having a very good hockey team, and, as we from Manitoba have found out, an equally good rugby team.
It is just about one year ago, Mr. Speaker, that a large part of the province of Manitoba, including the cities of Winnipeg and St. Boniface, suffered one of the most serious disasters in property destruction that has ever happened in Canada, through the flooding of the Red river. The generous response in material and financial aid from all over Canada, and from many places outside of Canada, was immediate, magnificent and generous. Among those first to offer aid in a very practical and generous manner was the city of Toronto, and as a Manitoban I want to add this as a further word of appreciation.
This acknowledgment is inadequate and far from being complete. We profited by every moment spent in Toronto, and, what is more important, we met and made a lot of new friends.
The board of trade of Toronto and all those [DOT]associated with our visit are to be compli-.[DOT]mented, both for promoting the idea in the first place, and, even more so, for the manner in which it was carried out. On behalf of the members of the House of Commons .and their ladies who made the trip we say: 'Thank you, Toronto board of trade.

I refer to that outstanding team, the Barrie Flyers. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an announcement of certain important changes in the high command of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Commissioner S. T. Wood,
C.M.G., has requested his retirement to pension, and will be succeeded by Assistant Commissioner L. H. Nicholson, M.B.E.
Due to the expansion of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, it has been decided to enlarge the directorate of the administration and organization of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police headquarters in Ottawa. The officer selected to fill this important position is Assistant Commissioner Josaphat Brunet, at present the officer commanding "C" Division, R.C.M. Police, Montreal.
The enlarged directorate will deal with the organization of the force and its distribution in the provinces, particularly with the eight provinces with which the dominion government now has agreements. It will also direct the training, apportion strength to meet the ever-changing needs, superintend the organization of staff and similar related matters, apart from actual criminal investigation. Assistant Commissioner Brunet will
30, 1951	2505
Royal Canadian Mounted Police be replaced in Montreal by Superintendent Noel Courtois, who is at present serving at Edmonton.
Other related changes will be as follows: Superintendent M. F. E. Anthony, the present officer commanding at Toronto, has been selected as the new director of criminal investigation at the Royal Canadian Mounted Police headquarters, and Superintendent J. Howe of Halifax is being transferred to take Superintendent Anthony's place.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to express the deep appreciation of the government of Canada for the magnificent service which retiring Commissioner
S.	T. Wood has rendered to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and to his country in the work which he has done while a member of this famous organization. He was practically born in the force. His father was Assistant Commissioner Zachary Taylor Wood. A graduate of Royal Military College, Commissioner Wood was appointed an inspector on November 1, 1912, and will complete exactly thirty-eight and a half years' service tomorrow.
Commissioner Wood has a wide and varied experience in the force. He was overseas with the R.C.M. Police squadron in the first world war; he has seen service in all parts of the dominion, including five years in the Canadian Arctic. Indeed, his case is a shining example of the fact that the high ranking officers of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police put in their full share of service in the difficult positions.
Commissioner Wood served five years continuously in the Canadian Arctic with headquarters at Herschel island in the Arctic ocean north of Aklavik, taking his wife with his first-born son as a baby in' with him. This son, Donald, later gave his life in the service of his country, being killed in action in the Royal Canadian Air Force in 1944 in Europe. The commissioner's second son, Herschel, was born just after they came out of the Arctic and was named after the island on which they had spent five happy and busy years. I have had the great pleasure of conversing with the commissioner about his experiences in the Arctic. I asked him if he were lonely there, and he said that on the contrary they were five of the most pleasant years of his life, and that far from being lonely he was very active and found himself with scarcely enough time to keep up with the arduous duties of a Royal Canadian Mounted Police representative in the Arctic. On occasion his duties involved taking patrols via dog team in which he would travel with Eskimo guides a distance of as much as 1,000 miles over a period

Royal Canadian Mounted Police of five to six weeks, sleeping in igloos built by himself and members of his party.
Commissioner Wood's second son, Herschel, was a member of the force when he recently met his death as the result of a motor accident. Commissioner Wood's third son, John, is now a member of the force.
Commissioner Wood had the advantage of studies of police methods in Scotland Yard, France, Belgium and the United States, and has occupied such important positions as director of criminal investigation and deputy commissioner before he became commissioner. In 1937 he had charge of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police detachment which was sent from Canada to the coronation of King George VI.
The period since March 6, 1938, that he has been commissioner has been one during which the duties of the force have been unusually arduous. The fact that Commissioner Wood had had first-hand experience in practically every province of Canada, and had had excellent police training, stood him in good stead during his thirteen years of the commissionership.
It is of interest that Commissioner Wood's great-great-grandfather was Zachary Taylor, the twelfth president of the United States. Before he became president, General Taylor, nicknamed "Old Rough and Ready", was famous as an Indian fighter and commander of the army of the Rio Grande. In this latter capacity he brought to an end the war in northern Mexico by an important victory over the Mexican General Santa Anna at the battle of Buena Vista. His victory on this occasion when his forces were outnumbered four to one by those of the enemy was so brilliant as to point to him as a candidate for the presidency of the United States, and he was elected to that great office at the next presidential election. He was president when he died in 1850. The American general and president will rest easily in his grave in view of the career, in one of the famous police forces of the world, of his distinguished descendant, Commissioner Wood.
Since I assumed the duties of my portfolio in November, 1948, it has been a privilege to have Mr. Wood associated with me in his capacity of commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. His work has been of immeasurable assistance, and I am glad to take this occasion of paying my personal tribute. Finally, in expressing appreciation of Commissioner Wood's service to Canada, I know that I speak not only for the government but for every member of this house and for the people of Canada.
A few facts with regard to the new commissioner will, I am sure, be of interest. Mr. [Mr. Garson.l
L. H. Nicholson, M.B.E., was born in Mount Middleton, New Brunswick, in 1904. He was a constable in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in his native province from 1923 to 1926, inspector in the New Brunswick provincial police from 1928 to 1930, and inspector in the Nova Scotia provincial police from 1930 to 1932. When the Nova Scotia provincial police force was absorbed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on April 1, 1932, Mr. Nicholson was granted a commission as inspector in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, which he has held to date. He was promoted to superintendent of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in 1940, assistant commissioner in 1946, and is now the senior assistant commissioner in the force. During the period from 1941 to 1946 Mr. Nicholson was on leave of absence with the Canadian army overseas, rising to the rank of colonel. He saw active service and was awarded the M.B.E. From 1932 to 1937 Mr. Nicholson was in charge of the criminal investigation branch in Nova Scotia, and from 1938 to 1941 he was in charge of the same branch in Saskatchewan. From 1946 until the present time he has been director of the criminal investigation branch, with headquarters at Ottawa.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RETIREMENT OF COMMISSIONER WOOD AND APPOINTMENT OF L. H. NICHOLSON AS COMMISSIONER  ENLARGEMENT OF DIRECTORATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am certain that every member of this house fully subscribes to the statement made by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that he felt he could safely speak for all of them in expressing to Commissioner Wood our admiration of the great service he has done to Canada, and in extending our congratulations and best wishes to the new commissioner who will take his place.
The office of commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police is one of the most important appointments at the disposition of the government. It is significant that the commissioner who succeeds Commissioner Wood served for some years in the criminal investigation branch; that seems to be the *line of succession to this extremely important office.
I am sure that all hon. members will agree that Canadians have every reason to be proud of the uniform of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Outside of Canada as well as in this country itself I doubt if there is anything that is more significant, both as an expression of something distinctly Canadian and as an expression of the respect in which we all hold those who are charged with the enforcement of law in this country.
As the Minister of Justice has said, Commissioner Wood comes from a family in which service of this nature was a tradition.

It perhaps is significant that Commissioner Wood received a considerable part of his training in the province of Saskatchewan, as has the new commissioner; and that is appropriate, because there is undoubtedly no single province in Canada more intimately associated with the history and tradition of this great force than Saskatchewan. There is in Battleford a museum which carries forward for the years ahead the great traditions and history of that force while it was such a steadying influence in the more primitive days of this country.
In paying our respects to Commissioner Wood for his splendid service in maintaining the efficiency of that force on such a plane as to call for the respect of all Canadians, we also extend to him and to Mrs. Wood our sincere wish that they may enjoy for many long years the retirement which he will now enter. I think it appropriate also that we extend our good wishes to a young member of that family, John Wood, who carries forward this great family tradition.
Commissioner Nicholson takes over an important post. He will occupy an office that will play a large part in the affairs of this country in the years to come. I believe there are a number of things about which Canadians have some reason to boast. I believe we have a right to claim that there is no police force in the world today which commands or justifies greater respect than the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. To Commissioner Wood our thanks go for what he has done to maintain its high standard; to Commissioner Nicholson our best wishes go for success in his new responsibility, and, in relation to the force in its expanded form as announced by the Minister of Justice today, for a continuance of the respect and confidence of the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we should like to be associated with the tributes which have been paid to Mr. Wood, and to say that we too have sincerely appreciated the efforts of this fine, outstanding public servant. Under Commissioner Wood's wise and able leadership the Royal Canadian Mounted Police continued to advance under a tradition that has been high throughout the whole world, and that has been the aspiration of a great many people. I join with others in expressing the hope that Commissioner and Mrs. Wood will have many years yet of happy, enjoyable living.
May I also express the hope that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and the government generally will try to carry on the improvements which Commissioner Wood attempted to make in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to better the conditions for the men in order to be able to attract into the force men of the highest calibre. That work was ably supported in this house, at least of late years, by the former minister of justice, Mr. Ilsley. I am expressing the hope that nothing will impede the progress of the force; that the government and the house will give to the new commissioner, Mr. Nicholson, every assistance in maintaining the high traditions of the force, and in particular, will help him to build up in this country the special investigation branch, which is more important than ever before in safeguarding the interests of the Canadian people in the face of constant threats of communist agitators and others who might want to cause trouble.
I wish to express my own personal appreciation of the fine way in which Commissioner Wood has always co-operated with us in any efforts we have made to improve the administration of justice throughout the world, and also to express the wish that the incoming commissioner, Mr. Nicholson, will receive every support from the people of Canada in carrying out his arduous duties.

subtopic: RETIREMENT OF COMMISSIONER WOOD AND APPOINTMENT OF L. H. NICHOLSON AS COMMISSIONER  ENLARGEMENT OF DIRECTORATE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a private member I wish to join in the tribute that has been paid by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), and by the leaders of the various groups on the other side of the house, to the work of Commissioner S. T. Wood, of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In my dealings as a member of parliament with Commissioner Wood I have never failed to appreciate his high sense of duty, his patriotism and his tact, and his knowledge of men, which was most helpful to him. He understood that the duty of members of parliament is to co-operate to the fullest possible extent with the commissioner of the mounted police in order to see that no abuse creeps into the dealings of the police with Canadian citizens throughout the country. Commissioner Wood has rendered countless services to the Canadian people in general, and many to my constituents in particular. I should be remiss in my duty if today I failed to rise, as I do, to pay my personal tribute to him on behalf of my constituents.
There is another thing, Mr. Speaker, that Commissioner Wood understood, namely, that men are not infallible. A great many people in the civil service and outside of it would never admit that anyone working under them could make an error or a mistake; everybody is supposedly infallible. They go so far as to give the impression that when a man admits an error or a mistake on the part of himself or of his subordinates, he falls in the esteem of his fellow citizens. Such is not the case. Commissioner Wood, on many occasions, personally redressed wrongs for which he was not personally responsible but for which some of his men were. He did that discreetly. He did not want anyone in this country to suffer any injustice at the hands of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. He understood that it was essential for the force to keep the respect of the Canadian people as a whole, and that such respect was in danger of being destroyed should any injustice be committed by any man in the mounted police force.
There was one thing that Commissioner Wood could not support, namely, the practice of a constable telling a person against whom a charge had been laid: You are accused of such and such a thing, plead guilty; do not see any lawyer. You will keep your job. You will be sentenced to a small fine and you will be much better off than if you go to a lawyer who will argue your case. Commissioner Wood understood that such a procedure is contrary to the elementary principles of British justice, and that everyone in Canada has the right to defend himself before the courts when a charge is

laid against him. This is one more reason why I rise today to pay tribute to the natural legal sense, the fairness, and the spirit of justice of Commissioner Wood. I hope that his successor will follow in his footsteps and will be worthy of the great tradition of the force.

should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman's information about the size of the last of these three fires is not accurate at all.

Order.

Unfortunately we do have fire losses in the armed forces because we have a very large amount of property across Canada which is in various states of repair, and many of the operations carried on constitute additional hazards. To keep down fire losses we have fighting services, excellent equipment, fire prevention campaigns and inspection by fire marshals. We know of no additional way in which more can be done to prevent fires.
With regard to the suggestion made some time ago by the hon. member that we use fire-resisting paint, which he may have had in mind, that of course has been looked into. We have estimated that we have 146 million square feet of buildings to cover, and it would cost $30 million to cover them with fire-resisting paint. We estimate that the balance of advantage would be not to use fire-resisting paint on existing buildings until we had fire losses in excess of $7 million a year.

Could you not put it on new
buildings?

That is done wherever it is considered desirable, but the advantages of that paint are often not nearly as great as are claimed for it.

The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 11, consideration of the motion of Mr. Fournier (Hull) that Mr. Speaker do now
Cost of Living
leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of supply, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew.

When this debate was initiated by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) on April 9, there was much shrugging of shoulders over on the government side, especially among the members of the cabinet. Apparently they thought that the motion was untimely; that it was a little bit unfair that a motion such as this should be introduced in the house just prior to the bringing down of the budget, which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had announced would be brought down on the following day, and which the members of the government had indicated was going to take care of some of the inflation which is abroad in the country. But when we read the budget, when we look over what the budget actually does, I ask hon. members if there is anything in it which will immediately effect a reduction in the present cost of living.
It is indicated at least by papers who are favourable to the government that that is not their opinion, because I see in the April 25 issue of the Regina Leader-Post a large headline which says: "Cost of living index likely to hit the 183 mark." When we are talking about this rise in the cost of living, and about points, you and I, Mr. Speaker, often fail to realize just what it means to the average person in this country.
The other day the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) placed certain figures on Hansard, indicating that in 1935-39 the cost of living index basket was worth $1,453; that is, the articles contained in that basket, purchased at that time, cost $1,453 a year. Since then we have had a rise in the cost of living of 80 points. That means that today we are paying $1,160 more for that same basket of goods than we were paying in 1935-39. That same basket of goods is costing us today $2,613. It may not mean so very much to members of this house who have a salary of $6,000 a year plus anything else we may have coming in; but I am telling you that it means a lot to the man or woman on an old age pension who can have an income of only $1,080. It means a lot to the veteran who is on a fixed pension; it means a lot to retired civil servants who are on fixed pensions.
As I said, there is nothing in the budget which would indicate that the cost of living index is not going to continue to rise. As a matter of fact I think I am quite conservative when I predict that the budget itself will cause a further rise of at least two points in the cost of living index, and when that is

Cost of Living
written into the price, the cost of living index in all probability will reach the all-time high of 185 points as compared with the 1935-39 average of 100.
Of course we would be in a terrible position had our income not risen to a certain extent during that same period of years. But the rise in income has been more than offset by the rising cost of living. When he was speaking to this motion on April 9, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) placed certain figures on Hansard. It is not my intention to repeat all of those figures, but on page 1739 he indicated that in 1946 the per capita income in Canada was $786. Now, when the cost of living index figure for that year, 126, was taken into account, it reduced that income in terms of 1935-39 purchasing power to $636.
In 1947 our per capita income had increased to $822, but our effective purchasing income had again been reduced to $607. In 1948 our per capita income was $919, but our effective purchasing income was $593. In 1949 our per capita income was $935; effective purchasing income, $578. In 1950 the per capita income was $962; the effective purchasing income, based on the cost of living index, was only $535. In other words, during those years our per capita income had increased by $176, but our effective purchasing income had been reduced by $101. These are startling figures. Just think; in that period of time, five years, effective purchasing income had been reduced, so far as the average citizen in this country was concerned, by $101.
What are we trying to do to offset the reduced purchasing power of our people? What is the result to those who are raising families and who have to go out and buy boots and shoes and the food, milk and other products they must have in order to raise a healthy family? They are entitled to a decent standard of living, but the result of the present high prices is that we produce much today that they are unable to purchase.
As I said before, it is all right for those in the larger income groups. It is all right for private members on the government side to shrug their shoulders and indicate that there is not much occasion for alarm in the rising cost of living. Certainly there is not much for them to be alarmed about personally. There is not much for the person who has invested in stocks and bonds to be alarmed about when he finds that they have increased in value. There is not much for the man in business to be alarmed about when he finds that his business has increased in value. There is not much for a man with a good farm to be alarmed about when it has increased in value. But it is a different

proposition for fifty per cent of the people of this country who are not even in the income tax paying group. They are the people who are vitally affected by this increased cost of living.
It is time that the private members in all parts of this house got up and said something on behalf of those people whose standard of living has been so radically reduced. It is time that something was done about it.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has indicated that he hopes to proceed with legislation with respect to old age pensions. I am glad it is the intention of the government to proceed with that legislation. However, I would point out that seventy-three per cent of those who are in receipt of old age pensions today are getting the maximum pension and will not get one cent extra by this legislation. Seventy-three per cent of those on old age pensions will be in exactly the same position as they were before. It is not going to help them, and they are the people who should be helped. It is all right to give $40 per month to everybody, but when we do that we should also be protecting those people whose maximum income is $40 a month. They are the people who are affected by this rising cost of living. It is the people on war veterans allowances and other fixed pensions who are affected. We cannot just shrug them off in this house, because there are too many of them. It is time we were doing something to protect people who need protection, who are not able to protect themselves because of their place in our economic set-up.
We all agree that the only way you can beat the rising cost of living is by increased productivity. What is this rising cost of living doing to the production of goods? I submit that in many cases it is reducing productivity. Take the case of the stock raiser. I know of many farmers who, having reached a certain age, decided to go out of production. They had dispersal sales, but not many young men attended those sales to buy stock. Why? The cost of production is so high that they just do not think it is good business to start a herd of cattle when it costs from $250 to $350 to purchase a breeding animal. The result is that many herds are being disposed of and no new herds are being set up to take their place.
Production is dropping. The same thing is happening in the dairying industry. In 1949 there was a reduction of sixteen per cent in the production of butter in Canada. The government are making plans to import butter next year because we are not going to produce enough for our own needs, in spite

of our resources and ability to produce. This condition is brought about by rising costs of production.
Many farmers are saying, "What is the use?" A man decides that he will not build an addition to his barn, nor will he increase his herd at present prices because there is no guarantee for the future. As a result we have a falling rate of production all through our economy today. In many cases this inflationary spiral is reducing production. Normally when prices go up people tend to produce more, but when we reach the point we have reached today, where the increased cost of production is so high, when there is no guarantee for the future, we find production being decreased rather than increased.
This applies as much to labour as it does to the farming population. We find escalator clauses in many of the labour contracts today to enable the worker to meet the increased cost of living. That has an inflationary effect. With a rising cost of living we are bound to have labour trouble. The average labouring man has to pay $1,160 more today for the basic articles included in the cost of living index than he paid in 1935-39, at which time the cost was $1,453. Every point rise in the cost of living means that it costs $14.53 more to buy the same amount of goods. The result will be greater demands for higher wages. We are just in a spiral. It is a case of the dog chasing its tail. Apparently the government are not prepared to step in and make the necessary adjustments or impose the necessary controls to stop this spiral.
I do not know how far they intend to let it go. Will they step in when the cost of living reaches 185? Will they step in when it reaches 200? Nobody knows what the intention of the government is. The result is that many people selling goods today are out to get the most that they can. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) recognized that in the speech he made in the early part of this session, when he said that there was a tendency to get prices up before controls were put into effect.
In my opinion the government should do what was done in Great Britain during the last war; they should have assisted in the production of a line of utility goods. I have seen some of the utility goods produced in Great Britain during the last war-clothing, boots, shoes, furniture and other articles. They were good, sound, reliable goods. They had some value. Today when the head of a family goes out to purchase shoes for his children, unless he is prepared to pay the highest price he will get a shoddy article. The first time the child goes out to play in
Cost of Living
the mud and water it will be found that the shoes are just paper. There is no substantial material in them at all. If the government were to develop certain utility lines of goods in this country of good quality and would provide that such goods would be exempted from sales or excise taxes, or if these particular lines of goods were subsidized, then at least the people in the lower income groups, those who are not paying income tax, would be able to clothe their families properly and send their children to school.
What is happening to the average man today with a family of four of five children? Even if he is getting $3,000 a year do you think he has an opportunity to give his children a high school education or anything more than that? It simply cannot be done. What is happening in large families today is that the children are having to take a job just as quickly as they can. As soon as they leave public school they have to find a job in order to help support the rest of the family. I do not think that is good enough in this country. I do not think it is necessary. I think that we can afford to give at least a high school education to the children of Canada, and that is more than the average family can do with the present cost of living. I think that action should be taken immediately in this matter.
Another point raised by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) had to do with the question of monopoly control and its effect on the cost of living. If I understood the announcement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) correctly, it was to the effect that even though certain monopolies might be under controls with respect to the sale of their basic materials, they could still be investigated under the Combines Investigation Act. Maybe they can be investigated but I will guarantee that action will never be taken against any of them as long as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) occupies his present position. He made that quite clear in 1946. We have a Combines Investigation Act, but up to date not one major combine has ever been investigated under the act. Certain smaller industries have been investigated. We investigated some of the bakers in western Canada, but when it came to investigating the milling industry that was a different story. They were a little too big, and we did not investigate them.
We investigated the flat glass industry. I ask you: How much do you or I spend on window glass in a lifetime? It is not very much out of our total income. We in western Canada spend a lot more on oil and gas for the operation of our farms but we have never heard of the oil industry being investigated,

Cost of Living
let alone any action being taken against it. Nevertheless every time there is an increase in the price of gasoline in Canada the increase is right across the board. It does not matter whether you purchase your gas from B.A., Imperial or some other oil company. You will find that the increase is the same right across the board for every company in the different areas into which they have divided Canada.
Is that unusual?

I do not know how they get the word around, but it all happens on the same day at the same hour. That is how the increases take place. There has never been one major industry in this country investigated by the government. I have made that statement on more than one platform and I am making it in this house today. Not one major industry will be investigated. The tobacco industry has never been investigated. The other day the minister brought down the budget and increased the tax on cigarettes by 3 cents. Nevertheless people have to pay 4 cents more, 25 per cent more than the increase in the budget. When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) was presented with the facts he said: I have nothing to do with it. That is the companies' business. We cannot interfere with their business.
Why have we got the Combines Investigation Act if we cannot interfere with some of these things in order to find out whether there is any reason at all for such advances? Certainly it is up to the government to see that the people as a whole get a fair deal. They should see to it that when they impose an excise tax or some other tax people will not have to pay not only the tax but an additional 20 or 25 per cent to some industry which may exercise complete control over that particular industry. We had an investigation of the farm machinery industry before the war. It was proven that a combine existed not only by the investigation which a committee of this house made but also by the investigation made by a committee of the Saskatchewan legislature. It was not a C.C.F. committee either. It was the good Liberal government that was in power there at that time, and which carried on the investigation.
A Liberal government.

A Liberal government. In the report of the committee they indicated that in their opinion there was a combine. There was never any action taken under the Combines Investigation Act to investigate the industry, nor will there ever be any taken as long as we have this government in power at Ottawa. They will investigate the smaller companies whose actions only affect a small

part of the total cost of the goods we have to buy. Until there is some control over the inflationary spiral, some control of companies that are taking advantage of the inflationary spiral, our cost of living will continue to rise.
What does this mean to the government? We have a program for the expansion of our armed forces on which we are going to spend $5 billion in -the next three years. We are going to spend that $5 billion for goods and services at the inflationary level existing in Canada at this time. What will be the result of that? The result will simply be that we will spend from $2 to $3 to obtain the same amount of goods and services as we were able ito get for one dollar in 1944 and 1945 when the war ended. For our $5 billion we will get less than $2,500 million based on the 1945 price index. It will cost us twice what it should cost us to rearm. Yet the government hesitates to pay subsidies to maintain price levels. In 1944 and 1945 it cost us approximately $200 million a year for subsidies. In the next three years it will cost the government $2,500 million more in what it is going to have to pay for goods and services in order to rearm. Surely we could spend a few hundred thousand dollars on subsidies in order to make a saving such as was made in the last war.
According to the then minister of finance, for every dollar we spent on subsidies we saved $12.50 for the people of Canada and for the government in the purchase of the necessities of life and the goods that we had to purchase to carry on the war.
Milk was only subsidized to the extent of 2 cents a quart then.
Two cents a quart to the consumer and 2 cents a quart to the producer. The producer received a subsidy as weE -as the consumer. There were two subsidies on milk.
It would cost a great deal more today to bring the price back to that level.

If we brought it back 4 cents it would be a big saving to a lot of people in this country. It would be the same saving of 4 cents as it was then although it would he on a higher base because the base has risen since 1945.
You would have to bring it back 9 cents.

I am not suggesting that we can roll back prices to 1945 levels. I am suggesting that it is time for us to step in and stop the inflationary spiral. I am saying there are ways in which it can be stopped. If we were to do today what we did during the last war, if we were to set the margin of

mark up that could be made by manufacturers, wholesalers and retailers, we would catch a lot of these people who are all set, and who have boosted their prices so that they are in a position where they can continue to make an unjust profit if prices are fixed at their present levels. Those people who have unreasonably boosted their margin of profit would then have to roll back their own prices, without the government interfering in their business. That is just one method that could be used, fixing the margin of mark-up. Then by subsidies, such as we used in the last war, we could certainly reduce the cost of living and stop the inflationary spiral still going on in this country.
If we do not, I do not know what is going to happen. People are losing confidence. As I said before, they are not increasing their production; they do not know where they are going from here. We find there is not the same initiative as when people felt more secure. That was how we got increased production during the last war; make no mistake about it. People felt some security; they could see they were going to get reasonable prices for what they produced the following year, so they went into the production of those goods and services. That is why during 1944 we were able to export almost 1,000 million pounds of pork and pork products to Great Britain. Today we have nothing to export. We were able to do that because there was a set price; people knew they could go into production on those commodities, and that there would be a sale for them at reasonable prices. We had surpluses of feed in the country at that time, and that was one reason for our increased production. The same situation exists today; we have a surplus of feed in the country following the last crop in western Canada. On the basis of that surplus we could have increased production if people believed they had any security. But as long as we have the present inflationary spiral, as long as this government will take no responsibility, we are not going to get production in agriculture or in many other lines.
What will be the ultimate effect of this inflation? It will be exactly what Stalin likes to see happen. It is a great pleasure to him when in a country such as Canada we refuse to face up to facts, when we refuse to protect our people in the lower income groups, and get into these inflationary spirals. It is a great help to him when the cost of raw materials reaches the point that we cannot be efficient in our re-armament program, and when many nations not so well off as we are are unable to arm at all. They cannot pay
Cost of Living
for the raw materials, so we have to give them what they need. That is the sort of thing that helps communism. So I say if we are to protect our people, if we are to have an effective rearmament program, and if we are to meet the threat of communism in the world today, this government must do something about the present inflationary spiral.

I wonder if the hon. member would let me ask one question. As a farmer I quite agree with his agricultural program, but how is he going to get the boys back on the farms with the higher wages and shorter hours in the cities?

Well, if the boy on the farm feels that he has some security he will stay on the farm. It is when he feels he has no security, when he cannot see what is going to happen tomorrow or next year, that he takes a job in the city. The farm becomes more attractive when there is some security. I can say one thing definitely; the boys will stay on the farms if we have a proper formula under the Agricultural Prices Support Act which will give them a feeling that they have some future security.

Mr. Speaker, coming from the farm I am very glad that point has been settled. In opening my remarks I should like to compliment a neighbour, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Murray), who made a great contribution to the debates of this house just the other day. I sometimes think we in different parties forget that when all is said and done the other fellow is not so bad after you get to know him. Then I should like to say, and I believe I am expressing the feelings of most hon. members, that I rather liked the idea of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) giving his parliamentary assistant the responsibility of piloting certain resolutions through this house. As one of the older members I must say I believe this sort of thing gives the younger members an opportunity to display their ability. I am quite sure that on both sides of the house there are many younger members who would be equally capable, but who unfortunately do not have the same opportunity.
I should like to say a word or two concerning the tobacco industry; I think it comes within the purview of what we are discussing, since it seems everyone is using tobacco. I do not know any other hon. member who could deal with the matter with quite the same background. I have grown tobacco; I have manufactured it; I have wholesaled it; I have retailed it; I have smoked it, and I have chewed it. I can hardly reconcile the

Cost of Living
statement the other day by the parliamentary assistant with respect to liquor with the situation we find today in regard to tobacco. My experience goes back to about 1920, and I am going to disagree with the minister on one point. I am sorry he is not here, but his parliamentary assistant is present. If I am not mistaken a Fielding budget in the early twenties gave wholesalers a rebate on the tobacco they had on hand when the excise tax was reduced, I think from $9 to $7.50 and then to $6. That was a precedent which might well have been followed throughout the years; and by not following it I believe this government has lost millions of dollars. I think that was the only time the excise tax on tobacco was first increased and then decreased. The other day the Minister of Finance said that retailers and others had to mark up their products when the excise tax was increased because they had to take a cut when there was a decrease. Well, to my knowledge that decrease in the early twenties was the only one ever made in connection with tobacco.
I am wondering if any of the officials of the department can answer this question. When they are after revenue and put on these taxes, I wonder if they consider only the goods in bond and not the goods in warehouse? If I were a smart manufacturer of tobacco and knew the budget was about to come down-I see some nodding over there as if there might have been some consideration of this point-I would warehouse two, three or four months' supply of tobacco. The members of the house have heard the member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) speak about the little tax stamp on a package of cigarettes which only indicates the number of cigarettes in the package. This is a mistake. This tax is costing the people of this country a great deal of money. As I said a moment ago, I can tell the Minister of Finance that if I were a smart tobacco manufacturer in this country-and these manufacturers are as smart as anyone in this country-I would warehouse as many packages of cigarettes with the tax stamp on them as would enable me to supply my distributors for three or four months. The government has lost millions of dollars by its failure to follow the policy of the early twenties of going into these warehouses. A great deal of revenue would have been collected.
It would not be fair for me, coming from western Ontario as I do, where in the last twenty years we have developed a tobacco growing industry, if I did not bring to the attention of the house a resolution which I received from the flue cured tobacco marketing association of Ontario. I do this because,

in the first place, the tobacco growing industry is comparatively new in this country. I shall only recite two or three figures, but in 1930 our production was 36 million pounds; in 1940, 64 million pounds; and in 1950, 139 million pounds. Most of that was produced in western Ontario, but there is a little cigar leaf tobacco grown in three counties in Quebec. I am saying this, too, because of a statement made by the parliamentary assistant (Mr. Sinclair), as recorded on page 2278 of Hansard for April 23. He said:
We have felt from an examination of our tax records that the point of diminishing returns has almost been reached so far as the liquor tax is concerned.
Then, farther down on the same page:
It was for these reasons that in this budget liquor was left untouched.
Now, a startling figure to me was the production of smoking tobacco in Canada, and taking that in conjunction with our increased population from 1940 to 1950 we find that we actually produced less in 1950 than we did in 1940. I have in my mind the idea that this excessive tax on cigarettes is going to be rather a heartache. I would not be surprised if it produced less revenue than the minister expects, and even less than it did last year. It does not seem reasonable that the government would leave liquor untaxed, and yet tax cigarettes in this manner, because someone in every household uses tobacco.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but it seems to me that this matter should be discussed on the budget resolutions in the committee of ways and means. We are considering a motion concerning the increased cost of living.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. If I may be so venturesome, I would agree, but I would say that out of the 262 members in this house, 255 smoke cigarettes. The increased cost of these cigarettes enters into their cost of living just as it does in the case of 99 per cent of the families in the Dominion of Canada. Today tobacco is not a luxury any more than a motor car is. I am not defending the tobacco industry, and I have not any interest in tobacco.
This association which represents such a large segment of our society in western Ontario has no doubt sent a copy of this resolution to the departmental officials, but I think, Mr. Speaker, it is fair to put it on the record. It is as follows:
At a meeting of directors of the flue cured tobacco marketing association of Ontario, held in Simcoe on April 12, 1951, the following resolution was passed unanimously. We view with alarm the recent increase in the excise tax on cigarettes . . .

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am very sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I believe that matter should be discussed on the budget resolutions.

Thank you; I shall abide by your ruling, of course. I shall be glad to go on at a later date, but I think the subject is of sufficient importance that it should be brought to the attention of the house. I know if you are in the chair that you will permit the discussion at that time. The parliamentary assistant or the minister may be sufficiently aware of what I proposed to say that some further consideration will be given to the matter.
When the Minister of Finance rose in his place on April 10 to give his fiscal accounting to the country, and at the same time counsel his countrymen what the year ahead held for them in terms of costs to be met and taxes to be borne, there were two primary considerations, two clearly defined problems to be weighed and solved. The first of these, of course, was the necessity of raising revenues to underwrite Canada's defence program and to advance this country's role in the North Atlantic alliance. All Canadians understood the threat that international communism presented to their way of life. All Canadians were prepared to assume new burdens of taxation, and all Canadians were prepared to sacrifice for national security, for regional security, and translated to the ultimate degree, for the preservation of democracy. They were willing to fight for liberty.
The second fundamental consideration was a domestic consideration, that of recognizing the extent of inflation in this country and introducing direct and indirect measures not only of arresting inflation but of alleviating its actual and grinding toll on public morale and on the public and private purse. Let us consider the effectiveness of the budget in dealing with these two phases of Canadian national life, Canadian security from wars and threats of wars, and Canadian domestic and economic security against forces and pressures, as scheming, as evil and as disastrous as those threatening physical attack and physical violence. The budgetary proposals of the Minister of Finance doubtless meet the first of these two tests, that of raising revenue. Certainly, in the year ahead, they will provide an unprecedented flow of tax dollars into the national treasury.
Let us now take a look at the second basic requirement of the budget, the need of concrete action to halt and indeed to reverse the pace of galloping prices-in a word, inflation. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that the cost of living issue has been dealt with in a previous
Cost of Living
debate in this house during this session. Because of that, sir, I scrupulously intend to avoid threshing what might be regarded as old straw.
No discussion of the budget, of the cost of living or of taxing proposals can be divorced entirely from a discussion of inflation as it exists in Canada today; and no discussion of inflation, it must follow, can be divorced from the cost of living in Canada, regardless of the subject matter of any previous debates in this house. Because, sir, while the budget and its provisions mean the added revenue necessary to finance Canada's preparedness drive and Canada's program of military co-operation with the NATO powers, by their very nature they aggravate and accentuate the one problem which they should have been designed to ease, if not eradicate.
Mr. Speaker, Canada's Minister of Finance, by his own words, in his budget speech, has indicted himself on a public charge of having uttered a bogus fiscal document, a worthless cheque drawn on the pay envelope and on the pocket of every wage earner and taxpayer in the country. That may seem to be a harsh interpretation, but it is no harsher than the impact of the tax increases announced by the minister, and which affect the cost of living today in Canada.
The evidence in support of the indictment is the minister's own case in justification of increased excise taxes on a whole range of consumer goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend; as a matter of fact, I just came in. But are we on the budget debate or are we discussing the amendment to the motion to go into supply? I suggest that it is not desirable that we should have two debates which completely duplicate each other. If my hon. friend is referring generally to causes in the country which relate to the increase in the cost of living, I suppose he is in order; but I do not think he is in order in discussing on this motion the details of my budgetary proposals.

Mr. Speaker, if I may be permitted to do so, I should like to say in all fairness to the Minister of Finance that I think he is perfectly justified in what he said; but I think he will also agree with me, that, after all is said and done, the budget, by whatever increases it may have caused in the cost of living, would have a bearing on the debate on the subject we have under consideration, namely the cost of living. I do not want to be out of order, and I hope that I may be allowed to continue.

Cost of Living

I must ask the hon. member to discuss the cost of living and not to discuss the budget or taxes, because if he does so we shall have a duplication of debate. May I read to the hon. member the amendment which is under consideration. It is as follows:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house is of the opinion that in view of the announcement made on Wednesday last of the greatest monthly increase in Canadian cost of living during the month of February to the disastrously high level of 179-7 points, immediate consideration should be given to the adoption of appropriate measures to hold down the cost of living and halt inflation."
Then I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that I am quite in order, to be quite fair; and I hope that the Minister of Finance will agree. I do not know how you are going to-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend would be quite in order to discuss the causes of inflation and the economic effects of inflation. But if he is confining his remarks to budgetary measures which can be taken to check inflation, then I suggest that his remarks in that respect should be made in the budget debate. I think he is quite in order in saying that the budgetary measures which have been introduced do not do anything to check inflation but rather aggravate it; perhaps he can say that. Of course I do not agree with him; I disagree. But I really do not think we should have a duplicate budget debate on this motion. We hear a great deal of complaint in this house about wasting time. One of the greatest time wasters is a duplicate debate. This is one case in which I think we might attempt to restrain ourselves.
Bring in a good budget, and we will not have any duplication.
I think we shall get along well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This was the real reason why I felt as I did about this motion. While I had no objection to its being made, I felt it was going to result in just the sort of thing we are getting today.

I think it is fair for me to say, Mr. Speaker, that inflation enters into the cost of living. I will try to curb myself in order to keep within your ruling. I certainly do not want to be unfair.
These tax increases presumably are intended as a deterrent to public spending and hence to inflation. These very increases fMr. Murphy.]
are calculated to provide a substantial portion of revenue which the government now requires to finance its way. In short, while the government and the minister profess to champion these newest imposts as inflationary curbs, they are fully aware that they will contribute little as a check to the upward sweep of prices. Indeed, should those tax boosts, by some strange chance, actually prove to be effective dampers to public spending, then the government would find itself in a sorry plight. The Minister of Finance, now estimating for a surplus of some $30 million, would find himself far short of balancing the budget, let alone rounding out the fiscal year with a debt-reducing margin.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I give up.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member discusses the budget specifically, I think he is out of order.

I would say, Mr. Speaker, 'that the spending of any public money affects the cost of living with respect to any citizen in Canada today. While it may seem strange to draw a line here, I cannot reconcile the viewpoint of the Minister of Finance by any means when he suggests that it is a budget speech. What else could it be, Mr. Speaker, when we are discussing inflation and the cost of living
We speak about the excise tax. All these taxes affect the cost of living today.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I said before, my hon. friend, like others, confuses cause and effect.
The original confusion was in the minister's budget.
I am going to have an 80-minute speech, Mr. Speaker, if these people do not stop interrupting me.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Judging from the number of sheets of paper that my hon. friend has, it looks as though it might be good for that.
I am glad to hear the minister say it might be good.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: For that, I said.

It would appear that the minister has little faith in what he professes-apart from the interruptions-namely, the effectiveness of the excise tax to stem public buying. I think that has something to do with the cost of living. One could venture the opinion, Mr. Speaker, that if the trend of public spending should surprise the Minister of Finance and his finance

department theorists, then members of parliament may anticipate another session this fall and another budget.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to have to interrupt the hon. member, but I must point out that his speech would be in order in the budget debate.
Put it in cold storage for a while.

I think I am perfectly right, Mr. Speaker, in indicating that if the anticipated revenue that the Minister of Finance has in mind is not forthcoming, there will be another baby budget this fall. I think I am perfectly in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That may be all right in another debate, but it is not in order in this debate.
Oh, Mr. Speaker-
I think we are discussing the cost of living here, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not so sure.

My point was with respect to inflation and these attempts to curb inflation, and I was saying that the steps that the government have taken might not be as effective as they presume they are going to be. If they are not, then I submit that we may be subject to a fall session and another budget. We have heard discussions in the house this session about the evenness of the taxation; that it applies to the poor as well as those in the higher income brackets. I would rather think that it constitutes inequity as well as iniquity, because those higher taxes and the increased burdens on those in the lower income brackets, as well as on those in the higher income brackets, make no allowance for the different spheres of the different peoples. It needs a little perception to recognize that the principle of a blanket increase works to the detriment of those with less funds, and they are the ones that we in this House of Commons are most concerned about. It bears less heavily upon the rich than it does upon the poor. I think that every member in this house will agree with me, Mr. Speaker, when I say that we are not very much concerned with those in the very high income brackets, but we certainly are concerned with those in the low income brackets.
The person on low or middle income now must assume the same financial burden as his fellow in the upper income brackets on a wide range of consumer durable goods that
Cost of Living
the government has described as luxuries. The range of goods against which the government has imposed new or higher taxes is open to challenge. I wonder if the electric stove in a modest country cottage or a washing machine in that same little cottage is a frivolous gadget. I am going to suggest to the Minister of Finance that when he goes home tonight he suggest to his good wife that they sell their washing machine for a washboard. I would advise him though to keep the front door open because it will not be the washing machine that will go out the front door.
It seems to me that today we are. taxed as a family unit, and the family unit is the very basis of our national society and our national economy. The government, through the Minister of Finance, has placed an excise tax on marriage. Young couples contemplating a home of their own must reckon not only with cupid but with governmental cupidity. In what I am about to say, Mr. Speaker, I mean no personal offence to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). He is not in his seat. I know that he has many appointments, but you will recall, sir, that during the last election campaign all the newspapers and all the magazine articles and photographs depicted the Prime Minister of Canada as the great family man, as the benign parent and grandparent. I have no doubt that there was a great deal of truth in those stories and in those pictures. Most men feel the same way about their families, about their children and their grandchildren-I know I do. I know that the leader of my party makes no secret of his affection for his own family. We are proud of that. But I cannot help but wonder, Mr. Speaker, how the Liberal government now reconciles the multimillion dollar publicity campaign it sponsored to build up that portrait of the Prime Minister in the public mind with the Liberal government's budgetary bludgeoning of Canadian families now established, and of young couples intending to establish homes of their own. Indeed, the government, through its taxing methods, tells young couples, intoxicated with romance-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is too much for the Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member once more, but he is out of order.
He should have made this speech on the budget; it is a good one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Intoxicated with love.

Cost of Living
Intoxicated with romance. I said it for the minister's ears. If he did not hear it the first time-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I got the gist of it.

The minister got the gist of it; that is the main thing. Indeed the government, through its budget, tells young couples, intoxicated with romance, to stay drunk. It is cheaper. And to this end it taxes stoves, furniture and home appliances. Someone said, not wood stoves. Of course that is one of these little blunders. To console them, it leaves alcoholic beverages free of further imposts. Of course the Minister of Finance will indicate that that has nothing to do with the cost of living. If it is provided free, as it was last Friday night, of course it would not. I hope that the hon. members who went to Toronto will come back and give us some ideas about what at one time used to be a Conservative city.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am glad you used the past tense.

I am glad you got that. What a travesty. What a cynical, iniquitous thing is this latest Liberal budget, and the various means they have found to increase the cost of living.
In his budget speech the minister emphasized that some of his proposals were to be regarded-I think this will apply to the argument that I propose to make-as an interim policy for the current year only. He said he regarded his tax-on-tax system as an easy and convenient way of raising revenue, a further admission that the government has its eye more on the number of tax dollars that it can amass than upon relieving any of the inflationary pressures now bearing down on the Canadian' family. But, Mr. Speaker, to leave aside the government's total disregard of inflation the total lack of budgetary steps to contain and defeat it by various methods, does it not strike you as inconsistent that the Minister of Finance at this late date can do no better than to enunciate an interim financial policy for this country? It is true that people in any walk of life today cannot look very far ahead when they are deciding on business operations, and depend more or less on government long-term policy to make up their minds as to what they should or should not do. That applies equally to those who may have to go out and buy necessary essentials for their homes.
In bringing before this house its military program, the government has set out a three-year program of rearmament and irecruit-ment. It makes no difference whether you have $10 or $10,000 to spend, you are budgeting. In its defence production program the

government has brought down legislation not for one year, not for two, three years, but for five years. In a whole range of ministerial speeches the Canadian people have been warned that the price of peace will come high, and that even though war may not come, Canada's defence preparedness will have to be maintained for many years to come. Plainly in the military sphere and in the realm of defence production Canada is being geared1 for a long-drawn effort to eliminate the threat of soviet imperialism. There can be no room for doubt on that score.
Yet despite all this the Minister of Finance tells the House of Commons and the Canadian people that we must wait for another year before he can determine which way the wind is blowing. If the minister is right in that attitude, then all the rest of the government is out of step with him. Or if government military and production planning for the years ahead is the proper course, and I believe it is, then it would appear that the Minister of Finance is out of step with the rest of the government. In other words, the minister should have placed before parliament and the people a properly reasoned and reasonable fiscal policy, not a twelve-months makeshift that he has been twelve months in the making hut which he can shift at will.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am sorry, but if the
hon. member continues along this line I shall have to ask him to discontinue his speech.

There are only two or three more items and I hope I can continue. I would not want to be out of order, but this is a very broad subject and I think I should be given the opportunity to go into many avenues with respect to the effect of the cost of living. I do submit that as the debate continues more latitude must be allowed to those who are endeavouring in their own way to show that the things I have been discussing have some bearing on the cost of living. I hope I can continue and I shall try to keep within the rules. If not, then I shall gladly abide by them.
The government has been dodging the issue of price controls. I am glad to see Your Honour smiling so I imagine I am in order. The Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and others have said repeatedly that they were convinced that such a system would not work at this time. They have insisted that a program of partial controls was doomed to failure. When I spoke in this house some few weeks ago I not only said that we should have controls but, and I repeat, I said that prices should be rolled back. I did not get much support for that idea from any part of the house.
Hear, hear.

I think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni-why doesn't he get a constituency people can spell?-agrees with me. They have insisted, too, that a program of complete controls would not work because of enforcement. Here again we have another display of Liberal government inconsistencj'. Harking back once more to the budget address of the minister we find these words, referring to the government:
We can restrain the expansion of credit; and we can apply direct controls either to particular conditions or, if necessary, more generally.
The government should make up its mind. Either there is inflation, or there is not. Either it can implement price controls to relieve that trend, or it cannot. This is the government that boasted during and after the war of its tried and proved experience and of the success of its price control policy. What do we find now? Out of all its vaunted wealth of experience and great leadership, what do we find? We find the government callously indifferent to the plight of the people, particularly those in the low income and pensioned groups, aggravating inflation, increasing the cost of living by taxation, and capitalizing, again by taxation, on the everyday requirements of Canadian families.
This is experienced Liberal leadership in this time of global travail. This is the steadying hand of the experienced Liberal administration upon the national economy. This is the crystal wisdom of the experienced Liberal administration as it counsels individual thrift and saving.
What an inspiring spectacle it is as this experienced Liberal government splurges the taxpayer's dollars on such things as the removal of the federal printing bureau to a seaside site in swimming Hull, as it controls and buys all the goods and all the materials, it requires for defence, but controls and stabilizes the flow and the prices of nothing at all that the public wants. What an inspiring spectacle of experienced leadership when it boasts of effecting a saving of several million dollars in governmental expenditures this past year and yet hands out $65 million on an unexplained basis to the wheat growers of the west.
What a magnificent picture of experienced Liberal leadership it makes as the government calls for more and more production and yet slaps a 20 per cent surcharge on the income tax of the worker who must work harder and longer hours to achieve the production the government deems so necessary. The splendour of that scene grows more dazzling as one looks at agriculture and the leadership that has been afforded in that
