Cost of Living
field. Experienced Liberal leadership has brought the dairy industry in all its branches to the verge of ruin-in the field of cheese production and butter production. The policy of this experienced Liberal government might be summarized in a single phrase, a policy of drift and be-I had better not mention that word.
For the pensioners of Canada and for those on fixed incomes the government has no word of comfort. To them during this inflationary period the government, this experienced government, says there is nothing it can do, that they must shift for themselves and eke out whatever existence they can. But I submit that there is something the government could and should do. For so experienced a government surely it would be no great task to establish the margin of profit mark-up permissible on foods and clothing, two great factors in the cost of living index.
I am sorry, the hon. member has exceeded his time.

Mr. Speaker, I presume it will not be out of order to discuss some way by which we may have some hope of dealing with the high-cost of living. One thing that is vastly desolating to a person sitting here listening to all the talk we have had thus far is the fact that mot a word whatsoever has been offered as to how the government can raise the money to accomplish the objectives which the hon. gentlemen appear to have in mind. If that is the only function of an opposition, then I must confess that I am amazed that the opposition is such a worthless, helpless affair.
Speak for yourself.

Exactly, I shall do so in
a very short time. If we face the situation which confronts us straightforwardly and factually we will realize that there has to be coming into the hands of the government much more money than even now is being contemplated from taxation and other reve-[DOT] nue measures which the government has in mind. What are we going to do about it? It would do me a lot of good to hear the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), with the experts who surround him, over on the government side proposing a budget. We could then see how he would do these things which the government is struggling rather earnestly-I would not exactly say desperately-to cope with. What I am going to suggest is something I have already suggested a great many times in the house, but something which in my judgment offers a real solution to the problem.
I do not wish to refer unduly to my C.C.F. friends, but as far as I can gather

Cost of Living
anything intelligible out of all that they say about financing, they seem to contemplate taxation in addition to what we now have. In other words, we find no evidence of anything but taxation in the minds of hon. members of two opposition parties who attempt to attack this problem. The taxation which these C.C.F. gentlemen appear to contemplate is, in my judgment, a kind of taxation which will discourage the production that we desire so urgently in this country. I think that puts it accurately and simply. I may be quite wrong but I do not think I am. I am trying to put myself in the position of someone who probably might risk a million dollars to establish a plant in an endeavour to produce goods for Canada necessary for the war effort, and who has to contemplate such a threat as C.C.F. ideas seem to pose before any such person in the not too distant future if they ever get into power.
May I bring to the attention of the house once more the question of the possibility of debt-free money created by the state, in accordance with the production of the country and the productive capacity, as a means of obtaining additional revenue which will aid in the financing of the nation's affairs without taking anything away from anybody and without hurting anybody. My general approach to that problem on this occasion is going to be more or less scientific. It is based on a study of financial history over nearly the 'ast two hundred years.
In my judgment there has come into the thinking of men in our day a strange species of fallacious concept with respect to debt-free money created by the state. I believe that if we are going to come through the dangerous times ahead successfully we must remove these fallacies which have come to be lodged so firmly in the minds of so many hon. members of the house and of the people throughout the country.
In order to show that I am not in the most disreputable company in the world when I propose debt-free money, may I quote a passage that appears in the annual report of the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, chairman of the Midland bank, to the shareholders of the bank as recently as 1936. This passage is to be found in the London Daily Times of January 30, 1936, right here in our library. I invite the leader of the opposition and every other hon. member to consider this quotation with the utmost care as coming from a man who undoubtedly is no crackpot, no matter what anybody tries to say. He said:
Additional currency, however, can now be furnished by the authorities, if they choose to exercise their powers without reference to the central

bank's holding of gold. Thus the nineteenth century, which brought into general use a means of payment hitherto scarcely known outside London, brought also the machinery whereby it could be subjected to intelligent control. We learnt that a shortage of money may be just as vicious in its effects as an excess, though deflation has still a touch of virtue about it in the minds of many people. Nevertheless it is becoming more and more widely recognized that greater productivity calls for an increased supply of money, for otherwise prices will fall, business will stagnate, and the growing productive capacity will be unused. For money to be truly "sound" there must be enough of it to finance an ordinarily growing volume of trade, yet not so much as to give rise to an inflationary movement of prices.	,
I do not believe there is a man in the Dominion of Canada who can successfully argue, in the face of that solemn statement by Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, that it is not feasible and intelligent to suggest in this country that we at least create some debt-free money through the finance department.
It will be argued that now is not the time to do it because relatively we have scarcity of production. With the information at my disposal, defective as it possibly may be, I am not prepared to admit that we have a deficiency of production over all in most of the essentials of our standard of living. If we have, then I maintain it is the business of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), or some other responsible man in the government, to explain to us exactly to what degree there is deficiency of production in this country.
May I now turn to another man who T think, will be recognized. I think the leader of the opposition will have to recognize this man. I wish to quote this time Mr. A. F. W. Plumptre, who used to be Professor Plumptre, writing in the Financial Post of October 5, 1940, on the topic of "Putting Over The Next War Loan". He said:
There are some general matters of theory which must be kept in mind in preparing for the next war loan. It must be remembered, primarily and seemingly paradoxically, that the government's object is not to get money but merely to reduce the public's spending. The government can always "get money" because it may, as an alternative to borrowing or even to taxation, create the required funds. This it can easily do nowadays through the leadership of the central bank and the co-operation of the chartered banks. In this way $200 million were created in this fashion last autumn.
I submit that if the opposition are going to be worthy of their salt they will have to ask certain questions and get the answers. One question that needs to be asked and answered is: At what stage of production in a nation is the creation of debt-free money and the circulation thereof justified by the production of that country? In other words, how much production need there be in a

country, or how much money can be in a country in relation to the production, before we are justified in creating money and putting it into circulation?
In my judgment that is one of the pro-foundest questions facing mankind today. What is the use of the leader of the opposition and dozens and dozens of other men in this House of Commons getting up and railing against communism and about the dangers of communism when they never give us the slightest hint of what can be done to improve conditions in Canada to enable us to offset the influence of communism within the country?
May I quote one statement which comes from another man who undoubtedly is worthy of high respect. I refer to Vincent Cartwright Vickers writing in a book called "Economic Tribulation", published in 1941, and which is available in our library. This is what he says:
Any additional supply of money should be issued as a clear asset to the state: so that money will be spent into existence, and not lent into existence.
That will be found on page 75 of his book. There is no doubt as to the meaning of those words. They are clear. Ten year old children can tell what they mean. I ask the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) if he cannot tell what those words mean. If he can tell what they mean, why does he not put in some study on the matter with which this gentleman was dealing?
Who was Vincent Cartwright Vickers? Perhaps hon. members will be interested to learn. We find this information in a note written by his daughter, Wilma Cawdor, and appearing in the front of the book:
Vincent Cartwright Vickers was born on 16th January, 1879, and educated at Eton and Magdalen College, Oxford. He was a deputy lieutenant of the city of London, a director of Vickers, Limited, for twenty-two years, and a director of the London Assurance from which he resigned in January, 1939. In 1910 he was made a governor of the Bank of England, and resigned this appointment in 1919. Later, he became president of the Economic Reform Club and Institute.
He died on 3rd November, 1939, after a long illness during which, against time and with failing strength, he was working and writing on economics.
The book he was seeking to finish was this very book "Economic Tribulation", as being the essence of this man's experience which he was contributing to the well-being of his fellow men. Does not the hon. member for Greenwood imagine this man's words are worth listening to? I am sure he would feel quite honoured if he could attach to his name all the distinguishing features which I have read about this man. So would any member of this house. I do not think the Minister of Finance, with all the jaunty assurance he 80709-161J
Cost of Living
possesses, would dare cross swords with a man having such a reputation without a great deal of very careful preparation.
Well, then, why do we find so many people who just will not pay attention to the words of men like Mr. Vickers, so well informed and' so well able to suggest a means of solving the problems of this generation? This book by Vincent Cartwright Vickers was written in 1939, before the war. Is it to be supposed that he intended his message to be of no value until a long time after the war, or did he intend it to be a valuable contribution during the war and the peace which was to follow?
The trouble is that the moment we make suggestions as to the use of debt-free money like those I have made already, we find people coming out with such words as "inflation". Many of them have not the faintest idea of what constitutes or causes inflation. The fact is that we have an inflation now, probably the worst in our history, after we financed a war with the soundest of sound money according to the most rigid orthodox principles the hon. member for Greenwood or the Department of Finance could imagine. The fact that we have such a terrible inflation now and do not know what to do about it ought to be pretty good evidence that their sound money ideas, according to the doctrines of orthodox finance, may not be quite so sound as they appear.
That is the thing we face. What has caused this inflation? The other day I listened to the leader of the opposition talk about inflation. Some of his remarks the Minister of Finance met with the expression "nonsense". I believe the minister was justified, because I must declare that the leader of the opposition was talking the most simple nonsense I have heard a man talk on inflation in the last fifteen years.
How would the Minister of Finance know he was talking nonsense?

He knew it that time, anyway. I wish the leader of the opposition were in his place, but he will be able to defend himself on a later occasion, and I shall be here when he does it. The point is this. Is it not a most alarming state of affairs when the leader of the official opposition in the House of Commons cannot even tell definitely and clearly what inflation is, what it means, and what causes it?
The other day the Minister of Finance said this inflation was a world phenomenon. Well, every one of the countries involved in this world phenomenon is conducting its affairs under orthodox finance, with which the hon. member for Greenwood is so completely enamoured. How in the world, then, has this inflation been brought about?

Cost of Living
Just to emphasize the truth of what I am saying, when the Bank of Canada was organized we were led to believe this would be a measure to protect us against inflation. Well, we fought a war under the Bank of [DOT]Canada. We have come through the war into the peace under the Bank of Canada. There are corresponding central banks all over the British commonwealth and in other countries, but notwithstanding that fact we have this inflation which is so serious as to alarm the bravest of us in this country. What is the matter? That ought to be enough to warn every member of this house that we just cannot treat these matters too lightly.
On April 19 I put on record a number of questions which were to guide those honestly seeking for truth concerning money, in their studies and thinking. The suggestion was definitely embedded in one of those questions the answer to which-if we would only learn the facts about finance and: not the fancies, with which we are being regaled so frequently by the presidents of banks all over this country1-would probably furnish the solution to many of our problems and show it to be right in our financial system. The longer hon. members study this matter the more they will realize the truth of what I am saying.
But now when debt-free money is mentioned If they do not call out "inflation" they scream "remember Germany", as though what happened in the inflation in Germany had anything on earth to do with debt-free money. They are referring to the German inflation, about which I shall have a little more to say in a few moments.
Those who have been informed by the deputy minister of finance and the men he has gathered around him as his cohorts and supporters will scream "fiat money", as it was used in the days of the French revolution. Their reference, of course, is to assignats, from the like of which they hope heaven will deliver us. A careful study of the assignat experiment will reveal much that can help us even today. The trouble is that the people who speak about that great experiment do not know the facts, and they will not take the trouble to find them. Instead, they permit themselves to be deluded by the deputy minister of finance. He is not here, but he is perfectly free to have his representatives and minions here in the house- and he has quite a number of them-disprove what I say. I challenge the deputy minister of finance and all his department behind him to contradict what I say.
If hon. members do not cry out one of these things, they will say, "Just think of

greenbackery in the United States under Lincoln! Heaven deliver us from that". Well, a careful study of the greenback experiment does not justify anyone in forming such an extravagant adverse conclusion, as I shall indicate shortly.
These four parrot cries, inflation, Germany, assignats and greenbacks, must be disposed of before any progress will be possible in our study of money.
If the hon. members of this house and the people throughout the country are disposed to be imposed upon by these four parrot cries, nothing can be done. But if they are disposed to probe into the problem themselves and get the facts they will not be imposed upon by these four parrot cries. These parrot cries constitute the first hurdle to be scaled before debt-free money proposals will be even listened to. But for any individual with an enlightened mind, free from bias and prejudice, these four parrot cries are easy to dispose of, easy to sweep utterly out of the way. In fact, they constitute no hurdle at all but rather an encouragement to us to probe into the possibilities of debt-free money.
Now, as to inflation; what is inflation? The leader of the opposition the other day evidently had in his mind three definitions of inflation, and they were all wrong, or at [DOT] least they were only right a number of years ago or right in accordance with the propaganda of the banks. It has been said that an increase of money is inflation. In one sense, we grant that is true, but no hon. member of this house will say the word "inflation" as we use it today means an increase in money. Then, it has been said that any undue increase of money that is unaccompanied1 by an increase in products is inflation. Well, that is coming somewhere near it. Another definition is any increase in money which is too great for the gold in the country that backs the money. The realistic definition of inflation has been literally hammered into the heads of everybody in Canada and the United States during two terrible wars as being, any rise in price, no matter what the cause or causes may be. Unless you do have a rise in price, any financial process is not inflation. What the leader of the opposition has got to do is to learn what inflation is, or he cannot discuss intelligently the present inflation, and all those who listen to him will just have their time wasted on this most vital matter. I could say a great deal more about inflation, but I do not think I will at the present time because I am busy with certain other things. I shall come back to inflation by and by,

whenever hon. members, including the leader of the opposition or the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), will question what I am saying.
The important matter before us now is, what part can money play in causing inflation? The answer to that is simply this: if we get into circulation more money than goods, as the hon. member for Greenwood said the other day, "when you have too many dollars chasing too few goods," that is the only justifiable monetary reason, as I think the hon. member for Greenwood will agree, for an increase in price. My question is: is that what has caused the present increase in price? I just raise one illustration, because I do not wish to go into too much detail. In April of 1946 the steel companies in Canada acting with government consent raised the price of steel by $5 per ton. Would the hon. member for Greenwood or the Minister of Finance or any other hon. member in this house say that was caused by too much money in circulation? Would the hon. member for Greenwood or the Minister of Finance or anyone else in the house tell us that you could make the steel companies take $5 off their price by taxing any amount of money away from the people of Canada?
The next thing that occurred, as all hon. members will recall, was that the steel workers struck for a share of that five dollar increase. The result was that the steel workers received an increase in wages, thereby increasing the cost to everyone employing them just as the increase in steel prices increased the cost to everyone using steel in manufacturing his product, directly or indirectly. Will anyone tell us that steel prices would be reduced or that wages would be reduced or that you can bring down the increased cost of living which resulted from those two factors, by a tax? Why, the very thought of it is preposterous, is it not? If it can be found that all the factors which have resulted in the great inflation we are suffering from are the result of incidents similar to that which occurred in the increased price in steel, will somebody tell me how on earth any amount of taxation in this country can reduce the cost of living? It is an absurdity! It is for that reason that I say the first thing we must do is know what caused this inflation; then we can set about seeing whether or not we can remove the causes or offset them. I shall have more to say about this later on.
May I just give a quotation to the house which will tend to establish the truth of what I have just said, that the thing which governs the amount of money which a country can have in circulation is the goods and
Cost of Living
services a country has in circulation or available for use in exchanges which people desire to make of these goods and services. Money is a medium of exchange as all people know. What do you need money as a medium of exchange for? To effect exchanges. When can you effect an exchange? When you have for example apples to trade for potatoes, or barber services to trade for railroad services or railroad services to trade for coal. In other words, the amount of money which you can have in the country depends on the goods and services you have in the country, and the disposition of the people in the country to effect exchanges. Now, the very minute you get that point dearly in your mind as a fundamental, you have to look on money altogether differently. The very first thing you will do if you want to find out whether we can create money and put it into circulation today in Canada will be to ascertain how many exchanges we are able and prepared to make in Canada. How many goods and services have we which we could exchange and have to employ money in the process?
I am going to read a quotation from a valuable little work by Sir Norman Angel] called "Your Money." This little work is in our library. The article was written when the Social Credit government went into power in Alberta. The Financial Post caused it to be written, and the general object of the dear old Financial Post was to scare people away from Social Credit. As a matter of fact, what Sir Norman Angell said was just the thing to show that Social Credit was completely sound in its attitude towards money.. On page 13 members will find the words which I am going to read, so they can read them at their leisure. You will find that I have not taken the quotation from its general context.
Now, it would make no difference to the valu? of Law's money-
By the way, Law's money preceded the assignats by a few generations. Law's money was a really wonderful experiment.
-that it should be "backed" by the resources of the Mississippi valley, or to the French revolutionary money that it should be a mortgage upon the national possessions, if the moneys were issued in too great a quantity in relation to the exchange of goods to be effected. Both of the moneys just mentioned became utterly worthless, although the whole resources of France and the French empire did "stand back of" them. If the quantity had been limited it would not have mattered in the least that nothing stood behind them in the material sense.
How sound those words are. I am sure the member for Greenwood can understand those simple words, too. I shall continue:
So long as they were legal currency, and their quantity was limited, their value would have been maintained.

Cost of Living
Which means that "backing" in the ordinarily accepted sense does not make a bit of difference to the value of the money.
What wrecked them was their excessive quantity.
No member in this house has advocated excessive quantity; certainly no Social Crediter has.
If the effect of putting material wealth "behind" money is to limit the quantity, to cause it to bear some quantitative relation to goods, the device, of course, serves the purpose of limitation. But it is the limitation of quantity which constitutes the guarantee of its value. Ricardo saw this quite clearly when he wrote:
"There is no point more important in issuing paper money than to be fully impressed with the effects that follow from the principle of limitation of quantity. It is not necessary that paper should be payable in specie to secure its value; it is only necessary that its quantity should be regulated."
May I break in here to ask once more: Quantity in relation to what? The exchanges which are to be effected in the country! And where is the man in Canada today who can tell us what is the number of exchanges that can be effected in this wonderful country? And what would be the number of exchanges which could be effected if you could put more money into the hands of consumers? And what would be the number that could be effected in the course of a year if you liberated the productive capacities of this country? These are the matters which in my judgment are matters of great importance and of great promise of hope as we approach the financing of the dangerous days ahead. I continue:
Now this truth, that the value of money depends in the last analysis, not upon the material of which it is made, or upon being "backed" by this or that commodity, but upon its quantity, opens up great possibilities for man.
I am endeavouring, Mr. Speaker, to canvass some of these possibilities before this house this afternoon. I continue:
He is not necessarily in this vital question of money the slave of a circumstance outside his control like the discovery or the failure to make adequate discovery of gold. He can control his money, make it his servant instead of his master, if he can learn the trick, the technique.
And the trick or the technique is learning how to measure or calculate the number of exchanges that can be effected and how to increase the possibility of exchanges and how to cause those exchanges to be made. I submit that just as soon as an effective study of this matter is made by the members of this house, the presidents of banks in this country, the presidents of mortgage companies, and all the other men who think they speak with authority, and are in a position where people listen to them, even if they are telling what is untrue, the better it will be; the important thing for those gentlemen all to do is to begin to examine with the utmost care these pages which I have put on record

of the writings of some of the most reputable financial experts to be found probably in the history of the world, in order to see whether or not something cannot be done to help this country and its neighbours, out of the difficulty in which everybody recognizes we now find ourselves. I have a great many things, which I hope to say regarding this matter.
I wish to go on with some more comments which have an important bearing on the whole thesis that I am attempting to develop.
I wish to refer to the German inflation. If all goes well, before we leave this session I propose to go into detail with regard to the German inflation and to give authentic information with which everyone will have to agree. Was the German inflation caused by debt-free money? I would advise hon. members to read Paul Einzig's book "World Finance Since 1914"; he is a gentleman who has in all probability known and told the truth; this is what he said. I am reading from page 47 of Paul Einzig's book that we find in our library:
In the case of Germany, inflation was forced upon the government by excessive reparation demands.
Did the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) ever hear of that? I will wager that he never did. I will wager that you could not get Dr. W. C. Clark, the deputy minister of finance, to acknowledge that unless you pounded it into his head. But there is the fact; and in due time, Mr. Speaker, if all goes well, and if the members of the house will permit me to do so, I will adduce evidence to support everything that Paul Einzig has said here. Meanwhile, may I point out these facts concerning the German inflation: Every mark was borrowed from German banks. Do hon. members get that? Every mark that made up the German inflation was borrowed from German banks in most acceptable orthodox fashion, to pay interest on Germany's war debts. Would the Minister of Finance or the hon. member for Greenwood object to that? That was good, sound, orthodox financing. Why did it cause inflation in Germany? Germany owed 147 billion gold marks internally at the close of the war, of which 58 billion was floating debt and 89 billion was funded debt. Would the hon. member for Greenwood advocate that Germany should have repudiated those debts? Or would the Minister of Finance have argued that Germany should have repudiated those debts? I do not think so. Would Dr. W. C. Clark have advocated such a thing? I do not think so. Then the question those gentlemen will have

to answer is:	How in the world could
Germany have managed matters in those times?
To make matters worse for Germany, this also happened:	The London conference
caused Germans to pay one billion gold marks in August, 1921; 362 million marks in March, 1922; and 254 million marks in August, 1922, to Belgium, a total of 1,622 million marks. I refer hon. members to Sir Norman Angell's "The Story of Money", page 345.
If you want the genuine cause of the German inflation, there is part of it-but just a part of it. At a later time, when I get an opportunity to do so, I will go into detail on the German inflation and I will quote authorities that no man in this house can question or will attempt to question. For men like bankers or anyone else in this country to meet the proposal to issue debt-free money with the cry "Germany" is for them to manifest ignorance, stupidity or downright hypocrisy; and I imagine that all three participate.
May we now turn for a few moments to the assignats experiment, the French republic's state-created, debt-free money? What caused the disastrous rise in price or the fall in the value of the assignat? Here are the general disadvantages under which the assignat functioned:	The thing that was
behind the assignat was a parcel of land, something like a quarter-section of land only smaller. How long would Canadian money maintain its value today if it had only a parcel of land behind it? That was what was behind the assignat unit of money. The word "assignat" means an assignment of land. Then every assignat was at least about $10 in value-$10 to $20. How long would Canadian money continue to keep up its value if the only denominations were $10 and $20 bills, and if there were no $5, $2 or $1 with which to make change? Then there was an unstable government which dared not tax. The government which issued the assignats was a revolutionary government which had just recently established itself and was not sufficiently stable in its position to enable it to tax. What would happen to Canadian money under conditions like that? And there was a disruption of industry at that time due to civil war which had been very costly. Then again France was under the blockade of Britain at that time, and British blockades in those days were pretty airtight; so that they could not get the goods imports which they had been used to. In addition to that, Mr. Speaker, the French people in France were fighting wars on all fronts. May I read a statement from "Monarchy or Money Power" by R. McNair Wilson,
Cost of Living
in which he is discussing the assignats. Here is a statement which the hon. member for Greenwood and the Minister of Finance, busy as these gentlemen are, will have time to read. Here it is:
The French had financed fourteen armies on their paper money-
So evidently it had not been worthless all the time. I continue:
Why should not other nations do the same? Consequently, as has been seen, the money power in every country of Europe exerted its utmost efforts to discredit the French paper money. Success was achieved by frightening the producers of food so that they refused to part with their bread and meat in exchange for assignats, which consequently lost all their value. This is the method invariably made use of to "crash" a paper currency.
Who are behind all the propaganda that is trying to scare us away from using debt-free money? The money power presumably. Who are behind all those banks and trusts that issue their specious talks? The money power no doubt. How many men in the department of the Minister of Finance are under the control of the money power?

And the fruits of the Department of Finance during the last fifteen years certainly have not indicated that they were free agents to do for Canada what they ought to have done. Just as an example, in 1935 when we Social Creditors first came here, when Canada's warehouses were literally bulging with food and her productive plant was probably only 70 or 75 per cent active, and over a million and a quarter men were unemployed, all of which were means of producing more goods than we produced, we should have had debt-free money. The Minister of Finance told us it would cause inflation. Well, in the light of what has happened since, was he not foolish? Who do you suppose told him that it would cause inflation, if it was not the deputy minister of finance, and who do you suppose deluded him? Is it to be imagined that a man, such as the deputy minister of finance, with the training that he has had, would not have had knowledge and sense enough to know that the creation, we will say, of $300 million, $400 million or $500 million of money in Canada, and putting it into circulation in 1934 and 1935, would have been beneficial completely and could not have caused inflation, when only just a few years later we had hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars liberated in this country, billions of them in fact, and they did not cause inflation. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not mean to come into this debate as early as this, but as there is a possibility that it may not last any more than two or three days longer I felt that I should say something, coming as I do from the province that was described this afternoon by the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Weir)-I may be a little wrong in the way I got his description-as the baby sitter province. It may be the baby sitter province, but it has also been described in such terms as the baby bonus province. The promotion to baby sitter province is rather pleasing to hear. The hon. member may have said baby sister province; I am not sure of that.
Oh, yes you are.

You should know that you
are better able to answer it. To me the subject is of such paramount importance, not only to this baby sitter, baby sister, baby bonus, bag of bones province that it may be if this present inflation continues, but to all Canada. Therefore I need no excuse for intervening in this debate for a short time.
T am not going to speak as eloquently as the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Black-more), nor am I going to try to become as involved as the hon. member became, and here I mean no disrespect, in trying to explain what inflation is. All I am going to do is to add my small voice to what has been said before so well by so many hon. members, especially those on this side of the house. Even though we have not heard it from hon.

members on the other side because they would not like to talk like this, in their heart of hearts I am sure they are bound to agree with all that has been said about the cost of living in Canada. If they are honest, as all hon. members are, they are certainly going to agree that there has been a tremendous increase in the cost of living in Canada.
The hon. member for Lethbridge asked: What is inflation? The hon. member said that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) could not define inflation and then he (the hon. member for Lethbridge) went on to show in various ways just what inflation was. Whether it is right or wrong, to me inflation means that there is more money coming out of my right-hand pocket, to use the vernacular, to pay for the ordinary things of life, the ordinary eating and the ordinary clothing of the people of Canada than there should be. That to me is inflation.
If we have to pay more for what formerly we used to get for cheaper prices, that is inflation. That may not be very descriptive of the real meaning of inflation, but if a great majority of the people of Canada feel that they should not have to pay as much to live in Canada as they have to today, then they must ask what is the cause of that. The cause of that appears to me to be an artificial raising of prices. How those prices were raised is beyond the ordinary mathematics that I know. I cannot possibly give a reason for it, but I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who is a very clever person, who is a very charming person, who is very well versed in these matters, will at some time during this debate come in and explain to hon. members of this house why this situation exists and why the government has done nothing about it. It is strictly a job for the government of this country. Whether we like it or do not like it, the only power in this country to take steps to control what everybody realizes, what everybody appreciates and what everybody is worried about, that is the cost of living all over this country, is the government.
It is all very well to say that the people who make good money need not be worried, that they are not kicking very much; but they have been taxed plenty. But what about these many thousands of people in this country today who must live on fixed incomes? I mean those people in receipt of pensions that were fixed when living was not as it is today; I mean people like those who are retired from the civil service, people who are retired from private companies, people who are retired from public companies.

There are thousands of people of that type whose pensions were fixed back four, five or maybe ten or fifteen years ago.
These people are receiving the same amount of money today as they were when their pensions were fixed. What becomes of these people? They get no relief in the income tax. Comparatively few of them need relief because comparatively few are in the brackets where income tax applies. But there are still quite a large number who have to pay the increased income taxes and who are still on these fixed pensions. It is those particular cases that I refer to now. What is to become of them? What is to become of the man or the woman in the lower income tax brackets, who does not pay any worthwhile tax? What is he or she to do about meeting the higher cost of living?
That is one problem that is absolutely right up the street of this government. Hon. members opposite know that. Let me say to them I am not speaking words of wisdom about it-I refer to war veterans who are receiving pensions and teachers who are on pension. What is to become of these people? Are we to say to them that this is a war effort and they have to put up with it? But how are they to live? It is all very well for hon. members to say that "it better be live horse till you get grass", but after all, these are human beings and somehow they must live. What is the government doing about it? I have not followed all the past debates. As some hon. members know, I have not been here all the time, and because of the rather irregular mail service we have in my province Hansard has not been delivered as regularly as it might be, and as it has been in other provinces. For that reason I may not have read everything that every hon. member has said, but from what I have read and from the newspapers I have followed1, it appears that the cost of living is exercising the minds of all the people of Canada, and indeed of all members of the House of Commons.
Whatever parties we belong to, whether we are on this side of the house or the other, if hon. members want to really speak their minds, one thing on which they have to be in common accord is the question of trying to curb what is happening in Canada today. That is why I call again upon the Minister of Finance, and call on him very deliberately, because it is his job, because he is probably closer to the whole situation than any other member, to speak on behalf of the government and say whether anything is going to be done, and if not, why not. Something definitely must be done. I do not suppose we can rouse the government from their lethargy 80709-162
Cost of Living
with respect to this matter. I do not know whether it is lethargy. They feel they have an obligation but they definitely do not feel that they should discharge it at this time, or if they feel they should discharge it there may be many reasons why they will not discharge it. I still say it is for the government to say why that is so. We have had excuses that if they control prices labour will not be satisfied, that labour is not going to play the game, that labour will demand an increase in wages.
That is quite true, Mr. Speaker. Labour is today, and justifiably so, demanding increases all along the line, and who blames them? Who blames the men of the professions today for asking for increased fees? Who blames anybody who is earning money today for asking for an increased amount? They must ask for an increased amount if they wish to live, and that also applies to our fishermen in Newfoundland. It applies to the apple growers of Nova Scotia, the farmers of Ontario and Quebec and the lumbermen all over the country. The government says: We are not going to control prices because if we do labour is not going to agree. To my mind that is a fallacy. I do not know too much about labour although I have been associated with labouring men in various capacities for some years, and again I am only speaking of labour in my own province.
So far as I am concerned, in talking with labour people in Newfoundland and up here -and when I say "up here" I mean the mainland of Canada apart from the island province of Newfoundland-I find that labour is not unreasonable, that labour is prepared to hold the line, provided prices are stabilized. You cannot blame them. How can you expect a man to go out and try to earn his living today, come back with his money at the end of his day, week, month, or whatever it is, and have to pay the greatly increased prices prevailing in this country today? The hon. member for Lethbridge made some remarks this afternoon to the effect that my leader did not know what inflation meant. As I said earlier, I know very little about it either, but there are certain figures that were given to me over the dinner hour that I should like to quote.
These figures have reference to Ottawa only. I am not going to quote too many of them but they are all the prices of essential food products in Ottawa today and as they were on the first of January of the present year. On the first of January butter cost 69 cents per pound, and today it costs 80 cents per pound. On January 1 eggs were 55 cents a dozen and today they are 69 cents a dozen. I wish we could buy them

Cost of Living
in Newfoundland at even that increased price. Milk rose three cents a quart to 19 cents a quart. Flour was quoted to me as having risen 4 cents for a 7-pound bag to 49 cents. The increase in a loaf of bread has been two cents. Lard has risen from 29 cents to 35 cents a pound; Canadian cheese from 49 cents to 59 cents a pound; tea from $1.15 a pound to $1.18; coffee from $1.08 to $1.18 a pound. Sausages have increased 14 cents per pound. Pork chops have increased 6 cents per pound, and the increase on hamburg has been 20 per cent.
I am not going any further into that list. I think these figures exemplify very well the great increase in the cost of living right in Ottawa. How these increases have been spread all through the country is very easy for hon. members from the various ridings to apportion. Naturally in my province the figures are entirely out of line. The original cost was greater and the proportionate increase has been greater. It may be that my leader does not know what inflation is in Canada, and possibly I do not know what it is, but the hon. member for Lethbridge will have to give other examples for me to be able to understand him. I do not mean any disrespect, but my idea of inflation, as I said before, is merely a rise in the cost of all things from what they were to what they are. That is inflation so far as I know.
I do not plan to be too long, Mr. Speaker, because I am sure other hon. members are vitally interested for themselves and for their constituents and will want to talk long and seriously on this matter. However, I want to reiterate something that has been said before. I am sure it has been said before because it stands to reason, because it is true. The other evil we have in the world today, apart from the rising cost of living, the other big matter that is exercising the minds of people all over the world, is the threat of communism. Like it or lump it, Mr. Speaker, whatever we say or whatever we do, communism flourishes in those countries where what is happening here now has happened before, where the savings of the people have been wiped out overnight, where the moneys that people tried to put away for their old age or for future illness went, as they are beginning to go here in Canada. Such countries were being prepared for communism. Like you, Mr. Speaker, and all other hon. members I do not want to see communism come in here. Quite recently an approximate figure was given us of the number of communists in Canada. I am not going to mention it, because I would be speaking only from memory and I do not want to do that; but we all realize it is a

very serious problem, and we all appreciate that communism is nurtured by conditions such as those now existing in Canada.
As I have said, the people of Canada expect this government to tell us why they will not impose controls. They say they will not, but they do not tell us why. The Minister of Finance must explain that; he must show the people why it is not necessary to have price controls at this time. So far I have heard no explanation. I do not suggest that I am a particularly bright person but I am reasonably intelligent, and as yet I have not heard nor have I read in Hansard any explanation by the government as to why controls should not be imposed. And that task belongs to the government. It is not the job of the official opposition or of any other party in this house to explain why that should not be done. We all have our ideas on the course that ought to be followed. I am not going to inflict mine upon hon. members, but it is up to the government to give us a full explanation. The people of Canada are the jury, and they can come to their own decision in the matter.
For a few moments I should like to go back to my own province and detail the situation as I have seen it during the past few weeks. It is quite true that a majority of the working people in my province, chiefly fishermen, do not pay income tax. That is so for the very obvious reason- that they do not earn sufficient money to become liable to the tax. But they certainly have to pay through the nose because of the rising cost of living. What is the answer? I came into this house with the other members from Newfoundland with the idea that we would do the best we could for what has been described as the youngest sister province. The bill of goods was sold to us this way in Newfoundland that if we came into confederation with Canada we would have a lower cost of living. Certainly that has not been the case. Today the cost of living in Newfoundland i-s higher than ever before. Of course I realize that the cost of living has gone up in the rest of Canada as well; but if you tried to tell the people of Newfoundland that they are living more cheaply than ever before they would not understand you.
By and large the economy of our newest province is based on fish. I hope I will still be in order if I discuss this matter very briefly, because it is part of this debate and part of the amendment proposed by my leader. The fishermen do not have to pay income tax, but unless the fishermen earn money they do not eat. If they do not catch fish -and sell it, they do -not eat. So if our newest province is to exist at all, we must

have assistance in connection with our fisheries; we must have a floor price tor fish in Newfoundland. Whatever else the government may or may not do, it must do that. I am not going to revive other debates; I am not going to talk about the $65 million that was paid in connection with wheat. I am only going to ask that some small amount be set aside to provide a floor price for Newfoundland fish for this year. At the present time whole settlements in my province say they are not going to fish because they cannot get an undertaking that they will be able to sell their catch at a fair price. What is the good of talking to these people about the cost of living? They cannot even afford to buy the ordinary necessities of life if they cannot sell their fish at a fair price.
We have been told that we were never better off than we are today; that when we came into confederation we had $42 million, and that this was a lot of money, more than we ever had before in our lives. That is quite true, but what is happening now? By the terms of union we are not permitted to use that money to subsidize the fisheries. So even if the provincial government had the money-which they have not, because they have spent it-they would not be able to use it to give the fishermen what they want, that is the promise of a floor price so they may go fishing again.
I am not trying to make any particular plea for Newfoundland as such; I am speaking for all Canada, but instinctively you speak of the only place you really know. That is why I am using Newfoundland as an illustration. This is going to be a very bad year for Canada's youngest province unless something is done about the price of fish. There are members in this house who know much more about it than I do, and I hope they will say the same thing I am saying, because after all they have just as much an obligation to the people of Newfoundland as I have. You know, the youngest sister always needs a little more consideration than the older members of the family. So I hope hon. members opposite and particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), who has always taken a deep interest in the new province, will bear these things in mind and see to it that whatever the economic situation this newest province is given a chance to live. We are not asking for money down there; all we want is a chance to sell our fish, a chance to live. That is all we ask. Perhaps I may be pardoned for again referring to Newfoundland, but I am worried about the financial position of that province.

You have been more than generous, Mr. Speaker, and I appreciate it. I will say no more on that matter at the moment but will let it speak for itself; and I thank you very much for your consideration. So, Mr. Speaker, all I want to say in winding up this matter is this. Like all Canadians, I am extremely worried about this spiralling cost of living. I do not care what any member in this house says today, I do not care what any member of the government says today, controls of some sort have to be instituted; otherwise the people of this country have to accept a much lower standard of living than that to which they are entitled. It is all very well to talk about being unable to do this, but still it should be tried. To me, this inflation is like a balloon. If you like, it is comparable to the Hindenburg which some years ago was filled with helium gas.
No, hydrogen gas.
All right, hydrogen gas. It was an inflammable gas.
House of Commons gas.

Perhaps it was House of Commons gas, which is an inflammable gas. Whatever the kind of gas with which it was filled-this cost of living gas, whatever it is, is no joke. I say this as I close, that this balloon that has been inflated is getting more inflated every day, and unless something is done to curb this inflation, then we shall have what happened to the Hindenburg as an example: it will blow up. Because of an accident but a preventable one. Then, what will happen to all of Canada? I think, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance had better explain what is going to happen when and if that balloon blows up.

Mr. Speaker, at this time I should like to add my voice to those who are taking part in this debate. I want to assure you that I support this motion in connection with rising prices. I am not going to cover the ground that has been already covered, only I want to inform the government that the constituency of Selkirk is suffering from high prices the same as every other constituency. Prices have now become so high that it is practically impossible for these people to maintain the standard of living that they had some time ago. It is going to be a black mark against Canada if we have to lower our standard of living. People who are receiving pensions today, not only old age pensioners, but those who purchased annuities so that they would have

Cost of Living
enough to live on during the eventide of their life, are being tremendously hard pressed. I could go over this ground again, but the members in my group and the members of the groups on each side of me have already pointed out these things.
It has been said that high prices are caused by the producer getting too much. I do not agree with that. Beef prices have been blamed for this high cost of living. It has been said that the sending of our cattle to the United States is the cause of high cattle prices. We have the remarks of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) at page 1759 of Hansard of April 9:
That is the only practical way I know of of preventing the price of beef in Canada from following the price in the United States.
I have been in the United States recently and I find that prices there are much lower than ours. I made a study of it. I went to different places in New York and other cities and I found that beef and pork prices are lower than ours.
I believe the Winnipeg Tribune, in an -editorial on March 6, 1951, hit the nail on the head. I am going to quote from that editorial which is headed "Those American Prices". It reads as follows:
For many years it has been accepted as an axiom by Canadians that the cost of living in the United States is higher than in the dominion. One of the reasons advanced for the current upsurge in prices by Ottawa spokesmen is that living costs here are simply following those of the United States. Few seem to have questioned these assertions.
Times have changed. Those familiar with prices of staple foodstuffs in retail stores south of the border claim that living costs in Canada, as far as many items of food are concerned, are substantially higher than in the U.S.

It was to be expected that fresh fruit and vegetables in the U.S. at this time of year should sell more cheaply than in Canada. But there is no apparent reason why many cuts of meat should cost more on this side of the line. Nor is there any apparent reason why margarine and shortening should be dearer here. Nor is there any obvious reason why eggs, milk and soap should be cheaper in Minneapolis than in Winnipeg.
For many years Canadians accepted as inevitable that motor cars, radios, electrical appliances and all sorts of gadgets were cheaper south of the line. They consoled themselves with the thought that it cost the people in the U.S. much more for food. Apparently Canadians are now deprived even of this consolation, if the above price comparisons mean anything.
Those who claim that Canadian food prices are simply following United States prices in the current upsurge are apparently talking through their hats- hats that would probably cost less in the States.
I believe that proves the fallacy of what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, that if the consumer wants to have cheaper beef we cannot sell our cattle to the United States. We are selling our cattle to the United States, and beef is cheaper in the United States than it is in Canada. The editorial I have just read proves that, and I have been to the United States and have seen it for myself. I have checked it. I made a special trip on Saturday afternoon to find out just what was going on. The producer is receiving more, but the price to the consumer is lower, as I was able to see when I was there.
I believe that the middleman or the wholesaler, the packer and the people in the middle are afraid that price controls are going to be established and they are making sure that the price is high enough when price control comes on. I am also of the opinion that the people who believe in the private enterprise system, as we have it today, are taking more than the traffic will bear; they are too greedy. For instance, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) put a three-cent tax on a packet of cigarettes; the next day there was four cents added to the price. There is no reason for that procedure so far as I can see. That sort of thing is going on right along the line. I could quote a few more examples where the tax has been put on and then just a little bit more has been added to the tax.
The old days of competition have gone completely, because everything is now run by monopolies. For instance, as to the packing industry in Canada, I think there are only about four firms which control the whole thing. If you go back through the records of the House of Commons you will find described how they meet in the morning in order to agree on the price they will pay that day. If that sort of thing goes on, the days of

competition are gone forever. You have monopolies and they are now so powerful that I sometimes think they have quite a strong influence on the government.
I have here in my hand an editorial which appears in tonight's Journal. Even the Ottawa people are seeing the thing as I see it. The editorial is headed "Prices Here and in the U.S.", and it reads as follows:
Washington, dispatches tell of further increases in U.S. prices of goods and farm products. The wholesale index now stands at 183-6 per cent of the 1926 average.
But let none of us have belief that living costs in the U.S. are higher than in Canada. U.S. rentals and food prices are higher, but not a whole list of other things that enter into the living costs of an average family. Textiles, clothing of all kinds, cottons, dresses for women, shirts for men, rayons and silks, household appliances, refrigerators, radios, motorcars-all these things are cheaper in the U.S. than they are in Canada. Indeed, since the application of Mr. Abbott's recent taxes, refrigerators, stoves
Order. I do not think the hon. member should discuss the budget at this time.
If I am wrong, Mr. Speaker, I will stop. But I am only quoting. I am not discussing the thing. I am giving the other-fellow's opinion.
I do not think the hon. member should do that at this time.

As I have said already, I do not want to do anything that is wrong. But I have not a university education as have some of these other hon. fellows, and I am trying to show that the cost of living in Canada is higher than it is in the United States, whereas we are being told different by the government. I have only three more lines to read, Mr. Speaker. May I read them?

I suppose I may give the hon. member that latitude; but the point I wanted to make was that we should not discuss the budget resolutions at this time, nor refer to them. Under the circumstances, however, I will allow the hon. member to quote the three more lines.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I appreciate your kindness. The editorial continues:
-and other so-called "luxuries" are considerably cheaper in- the U.S.
We hear much from time to time of the need of protecting Canada against U.S. inflation. A windowshopping tour in any big U.S. city hardly bears out such need; nor does a glance at the advertisements in U.S. newspapers.
I was bringing this editorial to the attention of the house in order to back up what I myself had seen. I do not think I need to say any more, Mr. Speaker. I have made my point, or at least I have tried to do so. Prices are
Cost of Living
still rising and the government do not do anything about it. The living standards of the people here and elsewhere are going down. That is a disgraceful thing to happen in this fine country of ours. I am going to appeal to the government to check these rising prices or to do something about the matter. In 1949 the people sent this government back to power, and the least the government can do is to protect them against high prices.

Mr. Speaker, I would be remiss in my duty to my constituents if I did not say a few words in this; debate, inasmuch as I represent a part of this country in which there is perhaps a higher percentage than elsewhere of people who suffer from any increase in the cost of living. To Vancouver island many people from the prairies and from other parts of Canada move during their ageing years; hence I find that in the outskirts of Victoria and on the southern portion of the island there is a high percentage of retired civil servants, retired railway workers, pensioners from the services -people who have accumulated small savings and have hoped to live on those in the milder climate. It is that class of people who suffer more than any other class when the cost of living goes up.
I do not feel that the situation is something which can be remedied overnight. The world situation as it developed1 after world war II does not permit of any easy or clear-cut solution. We are apt to be living in an age in which crisis and tension will follow one after the other, an age of great difficulty, an age in which sacrifices will have to be made by people in every walk of life. But if the Canadian people and those of the other free nations of this world are prepared to live up to the demands of this particular age, I believe that we may be able to avoid another era of blood, sweat and tears. If that be so, then I think we must look at the attitude of the people of Canada as a whole, not necessarily the attitude of those people I represent. Strange as it may seem and, perhaps, strange as it may be for an opposition member to say,
I do not believe that the majority of people in this country are concerned about the high cost of living. A great many of them are enjoying high wages. They are living right up to all their earnings. I would say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that it is not the high cost of living that the people are concerned about but rather the cost of high living. Until we can bring it home to the people of this country that they have to go back to the days in which the virtues of thrift and saving were recognized as virtues and not something to sneer at as belonging to an old era, we are never going to get a

Cost of Living
government that leads. The government are not leaders today. Any government are a flock of sheep. They follow what the people want them to do and they will say to themselves: Well, the people are not asking us to reduce the high cost of living; they are asking us to reduce the cost of high living. So you find that the government quite complacently goes along and says: We do not have to do anything about this. This is the situation which exists in the country. We do not mind very much about that small 10 per cent of the people who are really suffering from the high cost of living. And so perhaps it is wrong, or perhaps it is unusual, shall I say, for a member of the opposition not to take full advantage of pointing out all the errors of the government. I do point the finger of accusation to the people of Canada today and say that they are not really facing up to the situation, and that as soon as there is a demand from the majority of the people of Canada to reduce the high cost of living, and not the cost of high living, then the government, whatever party may be in power, will accede to their wishes and something will be done.
Some hon. members I presume are groaning with pain. I am sorry-
