speechtext: Pleased anticipation.

-if I have to inflict more pain upon them, but if prices do not come down pretty soon we shall all be in pain.
The reason I rise at this moment, Mr. Speaker, as I fancied the debate was going to close, was that I did not see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) rising to his feet, and I do not believe that this debate should close until we have an answer from the minister. Surely, when an amendment of this kind is sponsored by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Drew), and a debate has gone on for several days on a topic of such paramount importance in Canada today, we have reason to ask the Minister of Finance to answer the various charges and speeches that have been made on the amendment.
I get a little bit tired of this matter of coming down here and assuming that we are simply a debating society desiring to put things on Hansard, hoping that in the process we might perhaps get a little publicity one way or another, and pit one party against another. What we have in Canada today is a situation which is serious. That situation is explained in the amendment, and I do not believe that we should let this debate close without the minister satisfactorily giving 
us an answer, and an answer that is something more than an ethereal something that simply glosses the thing over or passes the buck. My leader whispers in my ear that the minister should not treat this matter with a conspiracy of silence.
We have a right to know. That is what we are here for. I do not believe that we should vote a dollar to the government until they satisfy us on these things. We know we are not voting money under the present motion, but there is more than one way of getting the minister to give an account of himself. We are trying to get into supply, and if he wants the money he had better come through with the answer. That is about the way in which we have to treat these things.
Surely the man who is responsible for the financial policy of this country, which policy results in the rising or lowering of prices, the amount of money that is in circulation, whether production is high or low, is the Minister of Finance. He is more or less directly responsible for that situation. He has his advisers. There is no reason in the world why he cannot give us an answer. It is not satisfactory to say that his answer is contained in his budget speech, because it is not there. Since he has his advisers, there is no reason why he could not say to this house: Well, now, if you really want to get down to brass tacks, if you really want to know the reason, we shall ask the banking and commerce committee to sit, and you can call in my advisers and they will tell you the reason for the high cost of living. That is, if the minister is not willing to stand before that committee himself, because somebody is behind the scenes pulling the wires, somebody is responsible for financial policy, and I think we should know who it is, and why they have permitted those things to happen.
Surely the minister must realize that he has an obligation to this parliament and to the people of Canada. I know what he says to us. Generally speaking it is: Well we are just one country of many and the situation is a sort of world-wide thing; just as though that excuses us. He reminds me of a song that was quite popular when I was a boy. I have forgotten how it goes, but I used to whistle it. The first line was: "Everybody's doing it."
"Everybody's doing it now."

Everybody's doing it now.
Well, simply because everybody is doing it, does not mean that it is right. Because every other nation gets itself into this same sort of mess it does not mean that we have to get ourselves into the same mess.
Or a worse one.

The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) spoke this afternoon, and he put some mighty interesting things on the record. There is no reason why the minister should not come through now and explain his position in the light of the authorities that the hon. member for Lethbridge quoted.
We live in an amazing country. We have a population of 12 million people.
It is 14 million.

We have a vast rich land and a great agricultural industry. There is no reason in the world why we should have to question whether or not we are going to eat tomorrow. I am not painting the picture too black. That is exactly what some people will be asking themselves if prices go any higher.
During the depression days we had a situation of unemployment. The old bogey was trotted out: Well, it is a universal problem. Just because other countries had an unemployment problem was no reason why we should have had it. But what happened? In those days goods were in abundance but people had no money in their pockets and the financial policy of the government was not able to take care of the situation. What happens today? Today people are employed; they have a bit of money, but prices have sky-rocketed so high that their money cannot reach the prices. So you have the same effect today that you had in the depression days. Surely the minister cannot absolve himself from responsibility in connection with those two features, depression in those days, goods but no money to buy them, and then today with money in our pockets we find prices so high that we cannot buy goods anyway. His financial policy is responsible for it. They did not have a policy in the unemployment days, and they do not have a policy now in the days of high prices.
The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) interjected to say that he did not have the university education that some other people have. Let me tell him that it does not take a university education to understand that you cannot buy meat at a dollar per pound with 75 cents in your pocket. As a matter of fact you might say that it is the university boys who have got us into this economic teeter-totter. Perhaps if they had a few people on the job who were realists and did not get mixed up with all these intricate things we would not be in the mess we are. We have the modern intellectual: more brains, less wisdom; more education, less knowledge.
Cost of Living
That is the situation. Quite often people come along to me and ask me whether I am a Social Crediter. I tell them I am and proud of it. Then they tell me that they cannot understand Social Credit. The first thing I poke back at them is something concerning our present monetary policy and I find that it is the present money system they do not understand. The things behind the scenes are so complicated that people are left in darkness concerning that very vital subject.
I am going to sit down, but first I say to every hon. member: We should demand of the minister that he give us an answer as to why his policy has permitted prices to rise and as to why his policy is not able to take care of the high cost of living. His responsibility demands that he tell this house why. Is the minister going to reply or is he going to sit still and indicate to the house that he has no reply?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am going to take only a very few minutes. As I said the other day, unlike some hon. members of the house I try to avoid repetition. It is three or four weeks since on the invitation of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) I expressed in language as clear and succinct as I could my views as to what caused the current inflation and what the Canadian government was doing about it. I do not propose to repeat those views tonight. During my budget speech I spent considerable time reviewing again some of the causes of the current world-wide inflation which, as I indicated then, so far as Canada was concerned was largely an imported inflation.
I told what the Canadian government was doing in order to counteract these inflationary forces on the domestic scene. I appreciate greatly the deep faith displayed by some members of the house that the Minister of Finance or any minister of finance can cure inflationary forces which exist in Canada or in the rest of the world, but I want to assure them that their faith is completely misplaced if they think that I or any other person in my position or any government can cure those forces.
I was particularly interested this evening in hearing the brief but excellent speech by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). With almost all that he said I am in complete agreement. I could not agree with his criticism of the government, but I was pretty well in agreement with the rest of the speech. One of the main reasons why we are having inflationary forces in Canada today is that every highly organized pressure group in the country is trying to make sure that rising prices are not going to affect them.

Cost of Living
On another occasion I made the statement that inflation is something more than an arithmetical fact, that it is a question of psychology and behaviour. Every time the costs of things rise, the highly organized groups in the country attempt to get higher wages or higher prices for their own particular products. They simply add fuel to the fires which we are trying to put out. I was particularly struck by what the hon. member for Nanaimo said. We cannot expect to superimpose a war effort of the dimensions we are now contemplating on an economy which is already fairly well employed without one of two things happening: either we increase our production or we diminish our standard of living.
It may be that some of the highly organized groups in the country will be able to maintain their position, but it will be at the expense of the people to whom my hon. friend referred, the pensioners, the people living on fixed income, people who are not highly organized. As I said the other day when speaking on the budget, the fundamental cure for this thing is for everybody to work harder and longer. We must do that if we want to maintain our present standard of living.

Mr. Speaker, there are several things which I should like to say about the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). Before doing that I should like to say to the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) that when he is congratulated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and applauded by Liberals he should beware.
The minister has asserted, not only tonight but upon previous occasions, that the inflationary trend within our country is a worldwide phenomenon, that it is imported. I am certain that if we were to go to the United States certain officials connected with that government would give the same answer, and the same would be true elsewhere. If that is to be accepted as a justifiable explanation for the conditions which prevail, then I ask: Is there any hope of solving it, or where is the start to be made?
Earlier this evening the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) gave his definition of inflation. I have no particular argument with his definition. All the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) did this afternoon was to elaborate upon certain fallacious beliefs which some persons harbour

in connection with inflation. He also elaborated upon certain very real conditions which lead to inflationary trends within a country.
This is the thing which struck me most' forcibly tonight. This amendment was moved on April 9. We have had the budget and prices are still going up day by day andi hour by hour. The government has made a substantial contribution toward that condition. True, we pick up our newspapers and find demands being made for higher wages. Why? When a man reaches a condition where his wife cannot pay the accumulated accounts at the end of the month then in the absence of a government policy to meet the situation he has no alternative but to demand more in the way of income. We pick up the newspapers and we find the railways, for example, asking for another 14 per cent increase in freight rates, something that could be wholly disastrous to the economy of western Canada and many of those persons in western Canada who today are confronted with the high cost of living in all its hideousness.
We have not only had the budget but I would say to the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) if he were here that we have also seen them fire General MacArthur, and that has not stopped the cost of living going up. Everything that has been done since this amendment was moved has had a tendency to force prices up and up and up. The pensioner, the person who finds it utterly impossible to meet the cost of the essentials of life today, is asking where it is going to stop. The same is true of low paid employees, and I dare say there is probably a larger percentage of them in the employ of the government than in the employ of any individual or groups of individuals. Why, Mr. Speaker, we even have to authorize some of them to go and baby sit in their spare hours in order to make enough money to meet the cost of living.
We have the widowed mothers, many of them trying to raise young families on $30, $40, $50 or $60 a month. We have our veterans of world war I and world war II trying to struggle along on pensions and war veterans allowances and their widows on allowances which have been granted to them We have many other groups whom it would not be difficult to mention. When I was back in the west during the Easter recess this was the common subject of discussion. The question most f requently asked me was: What does the government intend to do with respect to the problem of the present cost of living? I told them what the government had indicated as being its policy. I had to pass the comment

at the same time that I could not be convinced that their policy would have any immediate favourable effect upon the problem confronting them.
All one has to do is to examine certain available statistics to realize what has occurred since 1946. In that year we find that the cost of living index stood at 123-6; in 1947, 135-5; 1948, 155; 1949, 160-8; 1950, 166-5; and the latest figure we have for 1951 is 179-7. If this debate were prolonged for a few more days it is conceivable that we would have more reason for speaking with greater heat than anyone has spoken upon this occasion because it is my understanding that the cost of living index for the month of March will be issued in a few days. Then we will be able to judge the effects of everything that has been done up to this time to meet the situation.
A person having the average per capita income of $786 in 1946, on the basis of a cost of living index of 100, found himself deprived of $150 in purchasing power as a consequence of the inflationary condition. If he received the average per capita income of $822 in 1947, based on the 100 per cent cost of living index he would find that he had lost $215 as a consequence of the inflationary trend because based on the -cost of living index of 1947 his $822 had been reduced to $607 compared with the base period when the cost of living index was 100. In 1948, if his income was the average per capita income of $919, based on the cost of living index of 100, he would find that by the end of that year his $919 had been reduced in effective purchasing power to $593, a loss in purchasing power of $326.
In 1949, with the average per capita income at $935, comparing the base period cost of living index of 100 with the index for that year of 160-8 the $935 would be worth just $582, or a loss of $353 in purchasing power compared with the base period. Then we come to 1950 when the average per capita income was $962. Taking the cost of living index at 100 it would be worth $962, but since the cost of living index was 166-5 the $962 had fallen to $578, or a loss of $384 in purchasing power. Then let us take the figures for 1951 up to the time of our last cost of living index announcement. The average per capita income during that period was $961, but having regard to the fact that the cost of living index was 179-7 the $961 had been reduced to $535, meaning a loss in effective purchasing power of $426.
These figures, Mr. Speaker, can be applied to any income that you may desire to take. I simply took the average per capita income for each of the years from 1946 to 1951. It
Cost of Living
is when hon. members are prepared to sit down, take these figures and undertake to ascertain their meaning as applied to old age pensioners and pensioners of other types, those trying to live on savings and our low income group of employees, that they will see exactly what effect the perniciously high cost of living has upon these groups of people. We have said before and we repeat that there is every evidence that health is being undermined as a consequence, and every evidence that morale is being undermined as a consequence. Of course the effect of these two things can certainly be adverse so far as any defence effort is concerned.
Recently in a speech in this house I indicated that I had received a great many communications from one dry-goods dealer in a town in my constituency. Since that time I have added a great many letters to the nineteen which I had then received showing the tremendous increases in the retail prices of footwear and clothing since the first of the year. The increases run as high as 25 per cent. I think we all realize that in any family where there are a number of kiddies, clothing becomes a very important item in the family budget.
As things are going today the only apparent solution is to go to the constituency of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and join the Doukhobor sect known as the sons of freedom. If this keeps on I am afraid that is where many Canadians with low incomes will have to go. We know that the index for February showed the cost of foodstuffs running as high as 224-5 points as compared with 100 for the base period. It is my personal conviction that the most substantial item in the family cost of living, particularly where there are kiddies, is this matter of food. Merchants tell me today that their customers are finding it more and more difficult to meet their accounts at the end of the month. Not long ago it was my privilege to attend a dinner which also was attended by a group of twelve men engaged in the hardware, grocery, and other businesses. I asked them to tell me frankly what was their experience, and as I said a moment ago they pointed out that more and more people are unable to pay their accounts at the end of the month. I asked if that appeared to result from the fact that people were buying many things that might be characterized as luxuries. Their reply was that on the contrary there was every evidence that people were cutting down more and more, and purchasing only those things which could properly be regarded as strictly essential. Some of those merchants told me that in

Cost of Living
many cases there was a falling off of volume, that people were spending the same amount of money but were obtaining substantially less for it.
I asked one of these businessmen whether it was his belief that many prices had been hiked unnecessarily as a consequence of the government's failure to indicate definite action in connection with price control. He told me of an interesting experience he had1 only a week before. A traveller came into his store and indicated that the price of a certain commodity had been increased by fifteen cents. He asked the traveller if he thought that increase was justified. The reply was that it was not, but since the government had employed a policy of controls if necessary but not necessarily controls they had increased their price by fifteen cents, so that if there was a cut-back of five cents they would still be ten cents ahead of the game. That sort of thing has taken place in many instances. True, there are many business people who have not taken advantage of the situation, but there is ample evidence that a great many have. I feel very much as the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) expressed himself. We think we should definitely come to grips with this question and not just pass it off with the opposition voting for an amendment and the government voting against it, then allowing the matter to die. The hon. member for Macleod suggested that it would be a good thing if a matter such as this were referred to the banking and commerce committee of this house. Whatever else may be done I would urge that this course be followed. I am positive that as a result we would obtain some very enlightening and also very surprising facts.
I do not desire to take any more time on this occasion, Mr. Speaker. In conclusion let me emphasize that across this country we have groups of people who are finding it virtually impossible to pay their way. Only the other day I had a letter from an old age pensioner. Both he and his wife receive the maximum pension. He said that up to the present time, by cutting a few corners, they had been just able to pay their way, but that now they had reached the point where that seemed virtually impossible. If that was the case where both were receiving the pension, what must be the situation in the literally thousands of cases where only the husband gets the old age pension? Once again we urge the government to take appropriate action to meet this situation. The effects can be far more serious, as far as our nation is concerned, than some people seem to think.

Mr. Speaker, a few moments ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) outlined his own philosophy and possibly that of the government on this whole question of the increased cost of living which is bothering members of this house and the people of Canada so much today. As I understand his philosophy it amounts to this, that the cost of living will continue to rise as long as various pressure groups within the country continue to try to get more and more for themselves. That is nothing new; that has been going on since the beginning of time. The minister implied that people are pretty well looked after because most of them belong to one or the other of the pressure groups who are getting more and more for themselves.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, no, he did not.
There is one very important group which many hon. members have pointed out in the last few days is not looked after; that is people on fixed incomes, such as pensioners.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I must inform the hon. member that he has already spoken in this debate, and he may not speak twice. He spoke at page 1757 of Hansard.
I think you will find that I spoke during the budget debate, but not during the cost of living debate.
Sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member spoke on April 9 at page 1757 of Hansard.

Perhaps I can say a few of the things which were in the mind of my hon. friend. I listened with interest to the remarks of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) because the defence he put up, if it was intended to be a defence, was remarkably poor. The minister said he had not prepared it, and that I can well believe; but if he had prepared it I doubt if it would have been any better. There was no inkling or suggestion of a clue as to what the government was prepared to do about this tremendously vexing problem of higher prices and the rising cost of living.
The minister said there were pressure groups. I do not know what sort of pressure groups he had in mind; perhaps the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) could enlighten me. It would be very interesting to hear that the judges of Canada came down here as a pressure group to get an increase in pay or in pensions. I would doubt that such was the case; I rather think that out of the goodness of his heart

my hon. friend decided to give the judges of this country a little more money, of course thereby adding to the inflationary trend which the government has deplored. He is willing to do that for a certain group, which perhaps is not a pressure group, but he is not willing to do it for others.
There are two basic pressure groups in this country, of course. There are those who want controls taken off and kept off. That pressure group is made up of members of chambers of commerce, industrialists, managers of industries and entrepreneurs. That is the pressure group that has got the ear of the government, for the simple reason that the government is obviously the political arm of big business. There is another pressure group made up of the working section of this country, organized labour and organized agriculture, who for some time now have been asking that controls be reinstituted; but the government has turned a deaf ear.
There is a small pressure group made up of superannuated civil servants who are hoping to get some relief from the Minister of Finance, but they are not strong enough to be heard. There is a larger pressure group, but very weak, made up of old age pensioners who are hoping that some alleviation may be made of their tragic situation as it exists today, but they are not powerful enough to be heard; they are not powerful enough to be felt. So the pressure group which has the ear of the government is obviously that which wishes to see no controls imposed at all on this country.
It is true that organized labour wishes to see increases in wages when there are increases in prices, but the price increases always come before the demand for wage increases. The worker has to negotiate, to conciliate, to get his increase. On the other hand his employer has a perfect right at any time to raise the price of what he sells to whatever height he thinks the traffic can bear. The Minister of Finance said something else, a song which he is continually giving to us. He talked about the need for an increase in production. If we could get an increase in production, then prices would fall, he argues. My hon. friend knows as well as I do that production has been increasing in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But very slowly.

It has been increasing slowly or quickly, but it has been increasing and prices have been increasing. His argument, therefore, falls to the ground. Even though as he says the increase in production has been slow, nevertheless there
Cost of Living
has been an increase and there has been no corresponding decrease in the cost of living. It has been quite the reverse; the cost of living has gone up.
There is another factor in the government's policy which impresses me; I am sure it has impressed others. People realize today the dollar is becoming worth less and less. They realize that the dollar bill, as such, is losing value. They are determined, therefore, tc buy things because in things there will be some value. Therefore, by carrying out this deliberate policy of not imposing controls, the government is merely telling the people of Canada, "We are not going to impose controls; prices will probably rise and the best thing you can do is to buy those things which you need, and spend more". This is adding to the inflationary spiral which exists. There is only one political group in this country which I am satisfied is welcoming the government's decision, other than the Liberal party, and that is the communist party. They realize that inflation will hurt many people, will make them discontented, and it is on conditions such as these that the communists batten. They are amongst those who welcome the government's policy, a policy of inaction which is bringing nothing but misery to the people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, there arc one or two things which I think still remain to be said on this debate on the cost of living. Some of them arise out of a statement which was made a few moments ago by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), who adopted the attitude that, after all, this high cost of living is not peculiar to Canada; it exists in many other countries. It is, as it were, something which has been imported from outside; something which has descended upon us from the skies. It is universal, and the government really has nothing to do about it, no responsibility for it, and cannot do anything in any way to control it. There is a different attitude, Mr. Speaker, shown by the government with respect to anything for which they think they can claim credit. Then, of course, any good thing which descends upon this country, unlike the epistle according to Saint James, does not come down from on high but is solely and simply the responsibility of the government. All credit for those good things, according to the ministers who run this government, should accrue to them.
It is not good enough for any country, which carries on its affairs under a responsible system of government, for the ministers in charge of policy to say that this is some-

Cost of Living
thing which is a universal complaint, and tor which we have absolutely no responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No minister has ever said that.

I am glad to hear that, because that is a different impression from the impression given by the minister in his speech a few minutes ago. It is a different impression from that gained from the speech by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), and the Minister of Finance when he presented his budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just the contrary, he pointed out that there were certain things we could do domestically, and certain things we could not.
I am very interested in hearing what the minister says, but if he wants to answer he can make a speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have said that I do not go in for repetition any more than is necessary. Unfortunately, that does not go for my hon. friend.
Perhaps it is not worth repeating.
Perhaps, as the member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) says, it is not worth repeating.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That may be, and it is certainly true of a good many of my hon. friend's statements.

When the minister knows he has said something which really does not bear analysis and will not stand up under examination, then he says "Well, of course, I do not believe in repeating myself." It is probably just as well that he does not, because then the fact that his remarks do not bear analysis and do not stand up under the searching light of examination would become even more evident than when he first made the statement. He is not the only minister in this government who has said that this inflation is something about which the government of Canada can do nothing, because we have to wait for the United States or some other country-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No minister of the government has ever made any such statement.

The Minister of Finance
should perhaps read his own statement, and he should read the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have.
And he should read the statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent).

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I have, and neither of them
ever made any such statement.
Well, I recall very distinctly-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Quote Hansard.

The Minister of Finance is
never more effective than when he participates in debate from his seat. He is much more effective than when he participates in debate on his feet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He is good both ways.

Obviously something which
has been said here tonight is getting under the skin of the Minister of Finance, or shall I say getting under-well, quite obviously another portion.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Under his skin or under his seat.

The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said it. I did not like to be personal. I do challenge any hon. member of the government, or any hon. member in any other part of the house, to read a statement on this subject by a minister as to what might or might not be done to control the increased cost of living and prevent inflation, that is to say to take direct action by the government, and to contradict me when I say their attitude has been that one of the requisites that must exist before we can take direct action is for a control policy to be instituted in the United States, and for that policy to take some effect there before we can do anything about it. I challenge any other minister or any other hon. member of the house to deny that the ministers of this government have repeated time without number, by way of excuse, that inflation and the rising cost of living is not confined to Canada alone. It is not something about which we should be distressed because it is a universal phenomenon; that was the word used' by the Minister of Finance, and that was the description "universal phenomenon."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: World-wide, I think, was the word I used; world-wide phenomenon.

Well, to be accurate, worldwide phenomenon. I am glad the minister corrected me. I am glad he admits to having used that phrase which he sought to deny a moment ago. So that that statement, repeated as it has been by the Minister of Finance, who says he never repeats anything-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was just correcting my hon. friend. I was not repeating it, I was correcting a wrong quotation.

I am very interested in the
minister's distinction between a correction and a repetition. They have made that suggestion, and they have repeated it as though it somehow excused the government of Canada from the necessity of taking any

action to protect the people of Canada; as though the people of Canada are to relax and rejoice because they are not alone in their sufferings; as though we should find some consolation in the fact that we are not alone; that although the cost of living is high, and although suffering is caused to our old age pensioners, our retired veterans, retired service personnel and retired individuals who had tried, through their own efforts, to provide for their own retirement, even without government assistance, they should be happy because, after all, they are not the only ones who are distressed.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Better retire the government.
But then we have a Liberal government. They should take comfort in that.

Yes. As my friend the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) has said, the government's attitude-and this is about what it amounts to-is this:	Let these
people continue to suffer because, after all, there are others suffering in other countries, and those who suffer in Canada can always be consoled by the thought that they have not a socialist government such as the people have in England.

Or that they have not a coalition government such as the people have in Australia.

Or that they have not the troubles that the people have in New Zealand or that they have not the troubles that the people have in the United States where General MacArthur seems to be taking the centre of the stage. The government attitude seems to be that here our pensioners and our retired people on fixed incomes can relax because, although they are sharing the universal difficulties with other countries, they have that unique, outstanding and unusual blessing, namely, that they enjoy government by the Liberal party here in Ottawa. That is the attitude of this government. That is about all the hope and encouragement they offer to the people of this country who are suffering-and they are not suffering abroad or overseas; they are suffering here in Canada-from the high cost of living.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is nothing to what we are suffering from now.

I am quite sure the minister is suffering. The government do not like to hear people get up and criticize them. They do not like to hear people suggest that they

could do something to ameliorate the situation if they would really put their minds to it and if they would not give us platitudes. This is the government which during the war and during the post-war years said so distinctly and so frequently that controls were the answer, controls were the thing that saved the people from the higher cost of living, controls were the thing which countered inflation in Canada. You remember, Mr. Speaker, as well as I do, and as well as every other hon. member in this house does, how the government took the credit for and boasted about the effects of its control program. No one maintains that controls will cure the basic cause of the evil. No one denies that other things are required to cure the things which cause this rise in the cost of living. But the government, by its own arguments in previous years with respect to controls, is stopped from denying that controls would check the disease, or that controls would prevent the cost of living from going higher. Admittedly, controls are a drastic measure. Controls are a measure which no one welcomes except one group in this house, and I do not wish to get into a political or doctrinaire argument.
You had better not.

But no one, least of all the government that applied Lhem, can deny that they did check the increase, and that during a period of emergency they were applied for that purpose. This government tells us that we are in a period of emergency, and they call upon the people of Canada for efforts which they would not normally be called upon to make in peacetime with respect to economic as well as military and tax measures. That government should not, I say, shrink from its responsibility of taking those measures which would enable the people in turn to put forward their best efforts, secure and protected in the knowledge that while they were doing so-as it were, concentrating all their energies on the task which lay before them, and which the government ask them to accept-this creeping paralysis of inflation, this disease of a constantly-increasing cost of living, would not be attacking them through the back door as it is doing today. This government which talks so much about the universality of the present state of affairs, which says that they can dio nothing about it because the United States has not done anything about it, surely must have some answer to the fact that the controller of prices in the United States, Mr. DiSalle, speaking just a few days ago, said

Cost of Living
that Canada would have no alternative in his opinion but to apply controls when the full impact of the defence buying program hit this country. I should like to ask the government what steps they are taking to prepare a control program. We are supposed to be pumping $5 billion in three years into the stream of purchasing power in this country. Is that amount of money to be pumped in without any steps being taken to protect the people from the enormous inflationary effect that it will have? Are we to go along blithely waiting until some other country does something first? When are we going to reach the point where even the government will admit that the cost of living has risen to the point where something must be done? Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, why are the official figures on the cost of living index for the month of March delayed beyond the point at which they are usually delivered? This is the 30th day of April. To my recollection, the figures on the cost of living index for the previous month have never been delayed beyond the end of the month following.

Not of recent months.

On the sixth or seventh of April?

On the fourth of April?

Oh, oh.

You know, Mr. Speaker, we can make a joke out of this; at least the government can very easily, as they have just been doing, but it is rather more serious than that. The Minister of Justice shows no more interest in that matter than he has shown in this matter, or is shown by the other members of the government; therefore, Mr. Speaker, we can see through the attitude of the government, which they have shown in this debate tonight, that they regard this whole question as one to which they can show a supreme indifference, and one on which, when any member seeks to get information from the government as to what they propose to do, what are the facts
Cost of Living
upon which some action may be based, they take the attitude: Oh, well, after all, you are only a member of the House of Commons; you are only a member of the opposition, and what you say, speaking for the people of Canada, does not matter very much, because the government, even if they did know what the situation was, would not tell you, and if they told you they still would not do anything about it.
I was paired with the hon. member for Middlesex West (Mr. McCubbin). Had I voted, I would have voted for the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, before Your Honour leaves the chair and the motion before us is put, I want to call another matter to the attention of the house, namely, the near chaotic condition of the postal service in the Toronto and district area. We have raised this matter in the house before and have been assured by the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) and the parliamentary assistant that steps were being taken to correct this condition. On my visit to my riding last week I found that conditions are deteriorating more than ever in so far as that department is concerned. X speak whereof I know because there are more than 100 postal employees living within my riding.
Since the once a day delivery was instituted I have been in contact with the majority of these postal employees, and I have received representations during the past week from three associations of postal employees all insisting that matters, instead of improving, are getting worse. What is far worse than the undermining of the morale of the postal employees which has taken place is the disruption of the postal service. I had numerous telephone calls at my home from citizens, most of whom are carrying on their businesses from their places of residence. A number of them told me that they had been going as much as two days in succession without any mail delivery at all. Others have told me that they can have no idea now of the time of the day they are going to get their mail. It may be delivered in the forenoon, and it may not be delivered until after dinner at night.
I was rather surprised to find in the Toronto papers some ten or twelve days ago

a series of advertisements calling for mail carriers. When we were discussing this question in the house on an earlier occasion it was understood that the government's problem would be to find employment for those who were going to be relieved of their work by reason of the introduction of the one delivery a day. Instead of that we now find the government advertising for mail carriers. Some of those employed in the post office tell me that the department has been obliged to take men directly off the street without any civil service examination or civil service appointment and put them on the beats as completely untrained and inexperienced men to assist in mail deliveries.
What the mail carriers themselves have said to me is that in the first place they are still required to work more than an eight-hour day or a forty-four hour week. In spite of the longer hours there is no intimation whatever that they are to receive any compensation by way of pay for the extra hours worked. What is still worse, I am informed that the mail carriers are losing all interest in their jobs. I understand that a certain amount of clerical work has to be done by mail carriers in addition to delivering mail. I called some of this work to the minister's attention in a letter a few days ago. There is clerical work such as the re-direction of mail, keeping of records of changes of address and disposal of undelivered mail. I am told that these matters are now falling into arrears. Instead of being done at the time they should be done, sometimes they are left over for days or a week before being attended to.
The attitude the employees are taking is that if those responsible for the Post Office Department take the attitude that they are taking with reference to the employees, then there is just no point whatever in the employees themselves being more concerned about maintaining the service than are those officials responsible for it. Another matter has come to my attention. The one delivery a day is supposed to have been a bright idea that originated with the cabinet and was considered to be an economy measure whereby it would save $2 million or $3 million. I doubt very much whether that idea is the brain child of the cabinet ministers or anyone in the cabinet. In June 1949, the Canadian postal employees association through their national secretary forwarded a brief to the then postmaster general asking for certain reforms, changes and improvements in their conditions of work.
The postmaster general of that day, Mr. Bertrand, was away from Ottawa, and the deputy postmaster, Mr. Turnbull, replied to

the Canadian postal employees association in the name of the postmaster general. His letter was written on July 7, 1949, nearly two years before the cabinet conceived the idea of one delivery a day for economy purposes. The deputy postmaster general on that occasion wrote as follows:
In conclusion, I should again like to refer to the effect which further concessions would have on postal economy and which would inevitably bring in their train drastic revisions of present practices. These may include, for example, the reimposition of one delivery a day with lay-off of the surplus staff . . .
That was in reply to a brief submitted in June, 1949. That is the reply of the deputy postmaster general which to my mind constituted at that time a threat to the postal employees that if they persisted in asking for the forty-hour, five-day week, for permanent appointments for postal personnel, and for time and a half for overtime, they would have imposed upon them one delivery a day with lay-offs. That was the big stick which the deputy postmaster general held over the heads of the postal employees back in 1949. So I think one would be quite right in concluding with the postal employees organization that the application of this new order is simply the attainment of an objective which the deputy postmaster general, at least, had in mind for two or three years before it was introduced by the cabinet as an economy measure, and which was effectively used as a threat to keep postal employees from insisting on better working conditions.
I submit that the postal service as far as my particular riding is concerned has become so chaotic that nothing short of a thorough investigation by some independent committee will remedy it. I do not mind telling the Postmaster General that numerous postal employees in my riding are contemplating the possibility of going on strike and stopping the delivery of mail entirely. I suggest that is the last thing the Postmaster General would want, and the last thing the postal employees would want; but I assure him that the situation is becoming desperate. The minor improvements about which the parliamentary assistant told us the other day just are not meeting the situation. There are postal stations in Toronto where up to a week ago not a single walk had been checked. On many of the walks that were checked the supervisor was on the beat until nine o'clock at night before the delivery was completed. Many of those which were checked remain in exactly the same position as before.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister and the house; and I assure the hon. gentleman that something more than
Postal Service
the piecemeal efforts of the past few months is needed to remedy the situation.

Mr. Speaker, the point raised by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) has been before this house on previous occasions, and I should like to join in his plea with respect to the whole question of the Post Office Department. But I would not want to confine myself to the one area dealt with by my hon. friend, because I am not sure that the troubles of the department in that area are any worse than they are elsewhere.
I believe the government and the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) must have come to the conclusion by now that all is not well in his department. It may be that the minister will have some explanation to give with respect to certain moves he is making in an effort to rectify some of the conditions that now exist, but I feel that nothing short of a full airing of the department is going to quell the public indignation which has arisen following some of the changes that have been made. When you have rural Canada up in arms over the mail delivery that is being given, when you also find that the urban sections are showing great dissatisfaction, I think surely it is time we had the matter investigated by the special committee that has been suggested so often from this seat. I do not like to think the mind of the government is so adamant in a case like this that it cannot be changed, because I cannot see that from their point of view they have very much to be concerned about in reference to a committee. If the Post Office Department is all right the government need not fear any kind of an investigation by any members of this house. If the department is not all right then every member has a right to find out what is wrong and to suggest a remedy. It seems to me that is a very simple conclusion. I do not want to suggest that the Postmaster General is trying to cover up the troubles of the department by hiding behind the smoke screen so often employed by the government and saying it would not be in the public interest. If ever anything would be in the public interest, in that it would satisfy the public and clear the air, it would be an investigation by a special committee of this house into the operations of the Post Office Department.
I am taking the risk of again treading the ground which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) so carefully delineated today; that is, I am going to risk repetition because sometimes the only way you can drill anything into this government is to repeat and repeat and repeat. Sometimes they turn a

Postal Service
deaf ear in the beginning to some of the reforms suggested from over here, and then come to their senses later on. That is the one hope I have for the Postmaster General, and I express it now.

What I wish to say fits in with what has been said already by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy). I think the time has come when a good many matters in connection with our Post Office Department should be carefully considered and reforms instituted.
What I have in mind is that while a good deal can be said about the people who live in cities when they lose one delivery a day, and about the mail carriers who are losing some work as a result, I believe the worst treatment in connection with mail delivery is given those who live in small towns and villages, who have no mail delivery and who not only have to go to the post office to collect their mail but, if they want a box, have to pay box rental in addition. If we give free delivery in the cities, with the mail brought to the door and placed in the letter box, much more could be said for giving the people who live in the rural communities mail boxes without cost to the individuals who take the trouble to walk to the post office to collect their mail. Surely that should be apparent to every hon. member. I know that mail delivery in boxes comes to us from the early days of post office administration. It is something that has remained with us through the years and that we have taken as a matter of course. But I think the time has come when the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) and his officials should consider removing what I regard as an injustice and discrimination against those people who happen to live in the smaller places in Canada. I am making the suggestion to the Postmaster General that this is a matter which should be carefully considered, and this injustice removed.
I could talk about the people who carry the mail, and deliver it in the boxes that are located along the highways, the rural mail carriers, but I am not going to do that because an opportunity will be afforded when the post office estimates are before us. Since the delivery of the mail in the cities was brought before the house tonight, and quite properly, by the hon. member for York South, I am taking advantage of the opportunity of bringing to the attention of the minister the necessity for removing what I consider to be an injustice and a discrimination against the people-after all they are a very large

portion of the population-who live in the smaller towns across Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Since this discussion has been opened up in regard to the postal department, I do believe that this would be an appropriate point for me to refer to something which, previously, I have been able to deal with only by asking questions. I do so because it is something that does not apply to any one city, but which does require attention, and which does fit in with the suggestions that are being made for an examination of some of the problems that arise in connection with our postal service.
As many hon. members will recall, I have raised certain questions in regard to a situation which exists here in Ottawa, but which also exists in other cities across Canada. In Ottawa, there are a number of areas which have only been recently annexed to the city. In those areas there is no arrangement as yet in a considerable part for what is known as drop letter delivery. Representations have been made requesting drop letter service, but the answer has been given that in those areas which are not now receiving drop letter service the houses are not of the required density for a service of that kind, or the streets are not marked adequately to carry out that service. I am quite prepared to concede that there may be some difference of opinion as to what should be done in that case, but that does not answer the other part of the problem which seems to me to be utterly unjust and which should be attended to quite independently of the facts relating to the density of population or the marking of streets. In that, I am referring to the fact that in those areas letters require not a three cent stamp but a four cent stamp.
The people who live in those areas must put a four cent stamp on their letters, even if they are going to some other portion of the city of Ottawa. That might appear an injustice in itself, but what is a very real injustice is that in these days of postal advertising there are very few houses that do not receive a large number of circulars sent out to the household address or to people who purchase other things from some of the larger business houses. Quite naturally, those letters come out with a three cent stamp on the assumption that three cents will carry a letter anywhere in the city of Ottawa. I did not know that this point was going to be raised tonight or I could have brought here for this discussion a great number of letters that have been forwarded to me which are almost covered with postage-due stamps.

People who did not know that this was simply advertising material have been called upon to pay large sums of postage due, through the fact that someone sent letters to them thinking that they would be delivered in the ordinary city service. Many people, week by week, are called upon to pay a great deal in this penalty postage for reasons which are completely beyond their control, and representing no attempt, deliberate or otherwise, to disregard the requirement that four cents should be paid.
The answer that I received from the parliamentary assistant when I raised this question on one occasion when the Postmaster General was engaged elsewhere on the business of his department was to the effect that this was a statutory provision and that the Postmaster General could not vary that arrangement. I have pointed out by letter to the Postmaster General that since we are in session it is a simple matter for the government to introduce whatever amendment will deal with a situation of this kind. Other members who have spoken have indicated or have suggested that we have simply carried on from earlier days an arrangement which may have been perfectly satisfactory, but today conditions are much more complex in character. I believe therefore, Mr. Speaker, the Postmaster General should plan now to make an appropriate amendment so that this subject will be dealt with during the current session.

The
Speaker is quite capable of handling any situation that is out of order. I have some things to point out pertaining to my own riding, and particularly Haliburton county. For instance, there is only a three-day train service on one branch line going from Kinmount to Bancroft, and there is no railway mail clerk on that train. The mail bags are put on the baggage car, and thrown out at the different stations. From the time a letter is written until an answer is received from Toronto, it takes seven days. This is not very good service for a tourist centre which is developing rapidly. I am not asking the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) to inaugurate something that is going to cost more money, but something which will cost less money. The amount of money the Canadian National asks for hauling this mail now is far more than the cost of hauling it by truck. This would permit a daily mail service for less money, and it certainly would be a great advantage to the people living in that area.
Postal Service
I have a further grievance to take up with the Postmaster General in particular, and not so much with his department. A year ago a vacancy was created in the postmastership in the village of Bobcaygeon. The man who retired was eighty years of age. The day he was retired a young fellow was put in the post office by the department. After some seven or eight months a competition was held by the civil service commission, and the man with the highest marks in that competition-
But who failed on his written examinations.

No, he did not fail on his
written examinations. The Postmaster General knows better than that, because he and I have talked it over. I have had correspondence on it both with him and the civil service commission. As to this fellow who won the competition, I have the form sent to him by the civil service commission saying that he won it. I will grant you that the marks were close. He won by only 1-1 per cent. But nevertheless, the man who won the competition served six years in the army, five years of them overseas with the artillery, in Africa, in Italy and on the continent. The man who got the job was in the air force for eighteen months, two months in England with the ground crew. Of course neither of them received the pension, according to my understanding; and from the standpoint of the veterans priority, probably the young fellow had as much right to the job as had the other fellow who had the greater service. But nevertheless it was done on the authority of the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret). He told me himself over the phone that his officials had decided on this, that the younger fellow had been put in the post office; although I have a letter from him, signed by him, stating that the fact of the man being put in there on a minute's notice would not carry any weight whatsoever when the competition was held, but that the man who received the highest marks in the competition would receive the job. The man who received the highest marks in the competition received on the 29th day of May-or it was dated on the 29th day of May-a notification that he had received the highest marks in the competition, and that his appointment would be made by the Post Office Department on or about September 30. But that is something which never happened. I was down here on the 29th of September. In fact, I was down on the 28th, and it was two days before I got talking to the Postmaster General about this situation. However, I told him then that his officials had made this arrangement. The deputy postmaster general was not in

Postal Service
town and had not been in town, because I inquired. Who made the appointment, I do not know; but that is what was told to me. But I lay the trouble right at the minister's own door. He was head of the department, and I think he should not try to pass the buck on to any official. He told me that under section 24, I think it is-I am not sure of this because I have not the act here-of the Civil Service Act he is right for cause. I should like to know what the cause was.
Because there was a prior certificate issued by the commission.
I will show you the certificate issued by the commission. I have it in my office. I did not know that this matter was coming up, or I would have had it here.
There was a prior certificate issued in favour of the other man.

Two wrongs never made a right, and the minister should know that. If the civil service commission made a mistake on the first one, they certainly did not make any mistake on the second one; and they knew they sent the first one out when they sent the second one out. More than that, the minister overrode the civil service commission's decision under section 24, subsection (c) of the Civil Service Act. I should like to know what the cause was, because the man who did not get the job was recommended by the Canadian Legion.
Not from Bobcaygeon.
That was just three or four fellows who got together afterwards. That was three or four Liberals who got together afterwards.
Oh, oh.

That legion was not formed when this man was chosen by the Canadian Legion. It was the Legion that they all belonged to, maybe ten or twelve miles from that town, but that area was all included. He was recommended by the Legion, by the general commander, by his commanding officer overseas. He was recommended by the reeve of the town or village in which he lived. He was recommended by the mayor of the town and he was also recommended by the defeated Liberal candidate.
Surely; and he was recom-nended by you too.

I should like to know what ;he cause was that he did not get the job. That is what I should like to know. I should like the Postmaster General to declare himself on that point.
[Mr. Hodgsond
Then I wish to say a word as to the couriers in the town of Lindsay. I think it is the only town in my riding that has mail delivery. These men are heavily loaded with mail. The other day one man's mail bag weighed over sixty pounds. When a man starts out with sixty pounds of mail on his back, going up and down steps from house to house, it means a fairly hard day's labour. Some have been laid off there. I am glad to say they have obtained better jobs, probably at better pay. But if the Postmaster General saw fit to increase the price of second-class and third-class mail, whatever it was, he is probably within his rights. He has to make his department pay. We are not asking first-class service at the expense of the government. I think he was wise to make reductions to make the thing pay but I think it is a big mistake to cut down the couriers to the degree that he did.

Just following the discussion previous to this about the high cost of living, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I have had numerous complaints from the riding which I represent stating that the increase in the cost of mail delivery means a tremendous increase in the cost of living.
Order.
This is another instance of a hidden tax and I believe the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret)-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The debate on the cost of living has been decided by the house.

I am dealing with the post office. I will admit that you cannot eat mail or make a suit of clothes out of it, but it affects the postal department. My subject affects the postal department, when the rates for delivery are increased by one hundred per cent by the postal department.
That is not right.
What does it cost now to deliver the usual weekly notice from the church and what was the cost a year ago, if I am not right?
The over-all increase was not one hundred per cent.

If I am not right, are you right in saying that I am wrong when I say that the cost has been increased one hundred per cent? I still contend that I am right. I am not saying that the increase is not justified, but I am saying that people are complaining about that one hundred per cent increase. It is a one hundred per cent increase.

Any time this government takes it upon itself to increase the cost of living by one hundred per cent, through any department, I think the citizens of Canada are entitled to a lengthy andi thorough explanation of why this cost is increased by one hundred per cent. That is the question. These people want to know and they should know. If the increased costs are justifiable, I would point out that the public of Canada are long suffering. They have put up with this government for sixteen years, and I know they can take it. Surely in a matter of that magnitude, a one hundred per cent increase in cost of a department on any item is worthy of an explanation to the people. I can get no explanation, because apparently it is not in the public interest or we would have that explanation. I should not have to give it or try to give it, or try to explain it in any way. The explanation should have been given to the public long ago as to why such a drastic increase in the rate was going to be inaugurated or imposed on the citizens of Canada. What is happening to the money? Was it because of terrible inefficiency of the postal department prior to this drastic increase, or why was this drastic increase merited? Is it that there is to be some future terrific expansion that has never been known in that department before? The public should know. The opposition should know. If we knew these things, we would probably not be too critical; but we certainly have every right to criticize the great unknown, when the unknown is an increased cost imposed on thousands of people, to the extent of one hundred per cent on their cost of living.
PRAIRIE FARM ASSISTANCE ACT Mr. Solon E. Low (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I have a grievance that arises out of the administration of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act as it applies to the area which I represent in this house. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has been getting off pretty easy today, and I think perhaps this is just as good a time as any to raise this grievance and draw to his attention something that is happening. I think this is a justifiable grievance. I have received during the past three or four weeks scores of letters drawing this thing to my attention, and I have selected just one, which is typical of all that I have received, and I am going to refer briefly to the letter, Mr. Speaker, so as to draw the matter to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture. This letter is from Dimsdale, in the Peace river area, and reads as follows:
I am writing on behalf of seven persons all tributary to Grovedale post office. These persons,
Prairie Farm Assistance Act listed below, have been declared ineligible to receive P.F.A.A. benefits under an amendment to the act which declares any farmer ineligible who filed on a homestead after 1940.
The names of the people follow, but that is of no interest to the house. I continue:
Information furnished to the farmers union of Alberta by the P.F.A. people in Edmonton was to the effect that the amendment was only intended to apply to an area in the southeast corner of the province where people had been once helped by the provincial government to move out of a drought-stricken area to more favourable locations. No doubt you will remember the circumstances.
It appears that the vacated land there had been re-settled with the advent of more moist seasons. Then came more drought and constant application for P.F.A. benefits. Our information was that the amendment was to discourage settlement of that area. Now the amendment is interpreted to apply to all who entered on homestead leases from 1940 on. That does appear to me monstrously discriminatory.
During the spring session of 1950 an amending bill was passed through this house, and in the course of the discussion of the amendment on June 7 the Minister of Agriculture had these things to say, as reported at page 3310 of Hansard
What we say in the bill is that any lands that were not under private ownership at 31st December, 1940, are not to come under the act when they have been taken over from the government by some private person or organization. Lands that were still held by governments on the 31st day of December, 1940, do not come under the act as amended.
The intention is that any lands still owned by the government after some forty or fifty years of homesteading, and almost as many years when the lands were open for purchase and nobody thought they were sufficiently good either to be homesteaded or purchased during that period of time, are not good enough to be brought under this legislation after it is passed. That is the only principle underlying the bill.
In the Peace river country there are hundreds of tracts of land, still considered as crown lands, that were not opened for homestead purposes or for sale until recent years. As a matter of fact, they were not even opened for agricultural leases by the government of Alberta until the past three, four or five years. The reason that they were not opened for settlement was that the government of Alberta tried to profit from the mistakes that had been made in the earlier years of settlement of the west, during which time settlers went away out in the far-flung areas, many, many miles from cities or from existing services, settled there, built up towns and villages, and settlements and then began to howl for services. That was the kind of haphazard settlement that went on in the days of dominion government administration of the natural resources of the prairie provinces.
To profit by these mistakes the government of Alberta said: We will open only those

Prairie Farm Assistance Act areas that are contiguous to already existing services, and we will hold in reserve, even though they may be perfectly good lands, any lands which are not contiguous to existing services, and we will hold them closed to settlement until such time as services are near, or until it will be practicable to extend the services to them.
These lands of which I am speaking in various parts of the Peace river country are lands that were so held in reserve by the government of the province of Alberta. They discouraged homesteading and settlement in those particular parts of the country; and it was only when the boys began returning from the services, the army, the navy and the air force after the war that they began to make these pieces of land available for settlement.
Instead of selling the lands outright the government there decided it would be wiser to form agricultural leases and grant these leases to the returning young men and other young men who had not been in the services, but who needed to get land to establish themselves on farms, granting these leases for a period extending over ten years. The terms of the leases include clauses making it possible for the lessee to purchase the land at any time before the ten-year period is up for a specified amount of money. However, it is the scheme under which young men who have not much capital can get started on a farm. A great many agricultural leases have been granted by the province on property there, and in an area where drought rarely strikes.
Let me say this, Mr. Speaker: In the Peace river country, although drought rarely strikes, the people who farm these lands have to pay the rates on every bushel of wheat which they market, and therefore they do qualify for assistance under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, provided that they hold the property under the proper arrangement. When the minister put that amendment through last year I do not think he had in mind excluding from the act such lands as I have described to him. To support
my contention I am going to quote further from what he said, as reported at page 3310 of Hansard.
